editor.capcut-desktop.notes.1.t: CapCut’s pages state neither a size limit nor 1D support – the 33-point 3D cube is the safe file.

editor.capcut-desktop.steps.0.t: Select the clip in the timeline.

editor.capcut-desktop.steps.3.t: Apply it to the clip and keep “Intensity” at 100% for a technical log conversion.

editor.capcut-mobile.notes.0.t: CapCut’s own pages describe LUT import on desktop and web only; third-party guides say the mobile app cannot import custom LUTs.

editor.capcut-mobile.steps.0.t: CapCut mobile has no known .cube import – import the LUT in CapCut desktop (Adjustment > LUT > Import) instead.

editor.capcut-mobile.steps.1.t: Or bake the conversion into the clip first (see FFmpeg), then bring the clip to mobile.

editor.davinci-resolve.notes.1.t: Use “Open LUT Folder” rather than a typed path: the folder differs by install (sources disagree on Linux; the Mac App Store build keeps its own).

editor.davinci-resolve.notes.2.t: Resolve also reads the shaper cube (1D shaper + 3D lattice in one file, Blackmagic’s layout) – a shaped 33³ beats a plain 65³ on log footage. Other editors don’t: ffmpeg rejects it, OBS reads only its 1D part.

editor.davinci-resolve.steps.0.t: Open Project Settings (gear icon, bottom right) > Color Management > Lookup Tables.

editor.davinci-resolve.steps.1.t: Click “Open LUT Folder” and copy the .cube into it – a subfolder becomes a submenu.

editor.davinci-resolve.steps.3.t: On the Color page, right-click a node > LUT > your LUT, or drag it from the LUTs browser onto a node.

editor.ffmpeg.notes.0.t: lut3d reads 3D cubes only (a 1D file fails with “3D LUT is empty”), sizes 2–256.

editor.ffmpeg.notes.1.t: Never hand lut3d a shaper cube – it is Resolve’s format.

editor.ffmpeg.steps.1.t: Windows drive-letter path: escape the colon inside single quotes – lut3d=file='C\:/LUTs/x.cube' – or cd into the LUT folder and use the bare file name.

editor.final-cut-pro.notes.1.t: Apple documents 3D LUT import as .cube and .mga, with no size limit stated.

editor.final-cut-pro.steps.0.t: Select the clip, open the Effects browser > Color, and double-click “Custom LUT”.

editor.final-cut-pro.steps.1.t: In the Video inspector’s Custom LUT section, open the LUT pop-up > “Choose Custom LUT…”, select the .cube, click Open.

editor.final-cut-pro.steps.2.t: Set the Input and Output pop-ups to the color spaces the LUT converts from and to.

editor.final-cut-pro.steps.3.t: For log clips, alternatively: Info inspector > Camera LUT > “Add Custom Camera LUT…”.

editor.lumafusion.notes.1.t: Luma Touch documents .cube import “up to 64 points”, so LumaFusion gets the 33-point cube.

editor.lumafusion.steps.0.t: Copy the .cube to Files, or another location the app can reach.

editor.lumafusion.steps.1.t: Tap Import in the Library or the Color & Effects editor, choose the LUT, tap Open.

editor.lumafusion.steps.2.t: Double-tap the clip > Color & Effects > LUTs > User LUTs, and tap your LUT; keep the mix at full for a technical conversion.

editor.obs-studio.notes.0.t: “Settings only apply to SDR video” – OBS skips the filter on HDR sources.

editor.obs-studio.steps.1.t: Under “Effect Filters”, click “+” > “Apply LUT”, name it, OK.

editor.premiere-pro.notes.1.t: Premiere 25’s color management can already interpret log footage – check Lumetri Color > Settings so the log isn’t converted twice.

editor.premiere-pro.steps.0.t: Window > Lumetri Color, then select the clip in the Timeline.

editor.premiere-pro.steps.1.t: Basic Correction > “Input LUT” > “Browse…” and choose the .cube – a conversion belongs here, not under Creative > Look.

editor.premiere-pro.steps.2.t: Premiere 24 and later also offer Input LUT under Lumetri Color > Settings > Source Clip.

editor.soft.t: Menu names may vary by version.

editor.vn.notes.1.t: VN’s pages state neither a size limit nor 1D support – the 33-point 3D cube is the safe file.

editor.vn.steps.0.t: Copy the .cube to the device (e.g. the Files app).

editor.vn.steps.1.t: Select the clip > Filter > Add, choose the .cube, then a category or folder.

editor.vn.steps.2.t: Or from the Filter library: My Filters > Import Filter.

editor.vn.steps.3.t: Apply it from the category you chose in the Filter panel.

era.1860.tip.t: Before the standard observer: Maxwell’s and Helmholtz’s color triangles, three-color printing, the Munsell and Ostwald atlases.

era.1931.tip.t: CIE 1931 turns color into measurement – XYZ – followed by the first Lab spaces and NTSC color television.

era.1960.tip.t: Uniform color scales from the CIE and the OSA, Itten’s painter’s wheel, and the color signals of PAL and SECAM.

era.1976.tip.t: CIELAB and CIELUV make color distance perceptual, HSL and HSV put hue on screen, digital video gets YCbCr.

era.1990.tip.t: Rec. 709 and sRGB set the screen standard, Adobe RGB and ProPhoto widen it for photography, Cineon scans film.

era.2000.tip.t: CIECAM02 unifies color appearance, DCI-P3 defines digital cinema, camera makers ship their first log curves.

era.2010.tip.t: HDR and wide gamut – Rec. 2020, PQ, HLG – plus ACES for cinema, CAM16, and a log curve from every camera maker.

era.2020.tip.t: OKLab and OKLCH reach CSS, Material Design adopts HCT, log recording comes to phones.

faq.css.p1.t: Natively rgb(), hsl(), hwb(), lab(), lch(), oklab(), oklch(), plus color() for Display P3, Adobe RGB, ProPhoto, linear sRGB and XYZ (D65 and D50). CSS's rec2020 is a pure 2.4 gamma, not the BT.2020 curve of this catalog's Rec. 2020 – the same numbers would name a different color. Each dossier's css tab writes the current color in copyable form; spaces CSS lacks ship as ICC profiles or LUTs instead.

faq.css.q.t: Which of these can CSS write?

faq.cvd.p1.t: Open View and pick a Vision: red-blind (protanopia), green-blind (deuteranopia) or blue-blind (tritanopia). The catalog redraws as that eye sees it, so you can check that the colors of a palette stay apart. About 1 in 12 men have a color vision deficiency, by the NEI's count.

faq.cvd.q.t: How do colors look to color-blind people?

faq.exact.p1.t: Conversions are closed formulas, not lookup approximations, and round trips return within floating-point noise. The few exceptions are documented where they occur: OSA-UCS has no closed inverse, and atlas systems like Munsell interpolate between published grades. Output in rgb is never clamped: a color outside sRGB comes back below 0 or past 255, so clamp only when you display it.

faq.exact.p2.t: They are also checked: every space links the paper or spec it implements, values are tested against colorjs.io wherever the two overlap, and the camera logs against the Academy's official ACES transforms. formula-verification.md records what was checked against what – including a few places where the published papers themselves had errors.

faq.exact.p3.t: If the numbers differ from another library's, compare ranges: this one keeps each space's conventional ranges – RGB 0–255, Lab lightness 0–100, hue 0–360 – where many flatten everything to 0–1. Every card shows its ranges; in code they're space.oklch.range.

faq.exact.q.t: Are conversions exact? Do round trips lose data?

faq.gamut.p1.t: A color one space can describe but another – or your screen – can't show. A vivid Display P3 green doesn't exist in sRGB: convert it, and the numbers fall outside the valid range. The atlas keeps this visible: a ⚠ by the current color marks it outside the Limit you pick, Alt held over a plane or strip says which wider gamut a color there needs (P3, Rec. 2020), and out-of-range stretches ghost over a checkerboard.

faq.hex.p1.t: Type or paste it into the color field at the top, say #ff8000. Every space on the page shows that color at once; in OKLCH it reads 0.732, 0.186, 53, which CSS writes as oklch(0.732 0.186 53). Each dossier's css tab gives the copyable form, and in code it's space.rgb.oklch(255, 128, 0).

faq.hex.q.t: How do I convert hex to OKLCH?

faq.hsl.p1.t: OKLCH. It keeps the same three controls – hue, chroma, lightness – but its lightness is trustworthy: in HSL, yellow at L=50 emits about 13 times the light of blue at L=50, so equal L doesn't mean equal brightness. In OKLCH it does. CSS supports oklch() natively.

faq.hsl.q.t: What should I use instead of HSL?

faq.log.p1.t: Open your camera's log space, such as S-Log3, LogC4 or Apple Log. In its conversion LUT block, choose Rec. 709 and your editor: DaVinci Resolve, Premiere Pro, Final Cut Pro, OBS, ffmpeg and others. Your browser writes the .cube file. It is a technical conversion with no tone mapping: highlights above diffuse white clip, and the look is yours to add.

faq.log.q.t: How do I convert S-Log3 or another camera log to Rec. 709?

faq.model.p1.t: A color model is a shape for the numbers: RGB says three primaries, HSL says hue, saturation and lightness, CMYK says four inks. A color space ties a model to measurable light – which primaries, which white, which curve – so each set of numbers names exactly one color. rgb(255 0 0) is a different red in sRGB, Display P3 and Adobe RGB: one model, three spaces.

faq.model.p2.t: Everyday usage calls both spaces – so does CSS's color-mix(in hsl, …), and so does this catalog. A model without an anchor of its own borrows one: HSL and HSV here reshape sRGB, as in CSS.

faq.model.q.t: Color model or color space – what's the difference?

faq.muddy.p1.t: Because they're computed in gamma-encoded sRGB, where averaging two colors' numbers produces darker, duller light than actually mixing their light would. Interpolating in OKLab avoids this; in CSS that's linear-gradient(in oklab, red, blue). Every dossier's interpolate row draws the same blend through two spaces side by side, so you can see the difference before choosing.

faq.muddy.q.t: Why do my gradients turn muddy in the middle?

faq.pantone.p1.t: Those are licensed products: their colors are defined by data the owners sell, not by published formulas – so there's no open math to implement, and redistributing their tables wouldn't be legal. Close relatives whose math is public are here: Munsell (its 1943 renotation is public record) and RAL Design (defined directly in CIELAB). Any system whose math was ever published belongs here; suggest one that's missing.

faq.photo.p1.t: For the web and for sharing, sRGB: browsers and phones assume it when a file carries no profile. Display P3 keeps more of a vivid scene on Apple and many Android screens, as long as the profile stays embedded. Send Adobe RGB when a print lab asks for it. Keep ProPhoto RGB for 16-bit editing: its gamut is so wide that 8-bit files band.

faq.photo.q.t: Which color space should I export photos in?

faq.print.p1.t: A screen emits light; paper reflects what its inks don't absorb. Ink on paper reaches fewer vivid colors – saturated RGB blues, greens and reds fall outside it – so they print duller. Prepress converts through an ICC profile made for the press and paper, such as FOGRA39 for European coated stock or GRACoL in the US. This catalog's CMYK is the plain formula CSS uses for device-cmyk() without a profile – right for the numbers, not a proof of the print.

faq.print.q.t: Why does print look duller than the screen?

faq.what.p1.t: A coordinate system for color: axes, ranges, and a rule tying the numbers to measurable light. Human vision is trichromatic, with three types of cone cells (S, M, L), so three coordinates are the minimum to describe any color the eye can see. The same orange is rgb(255 128 0), oklch(0.732 0.186 53) and XYZ [49, 36.7, 4.5]. A palette is a handful of chosen colors; a space is a way to write down any color at all.

faq.which.li1.t: storing and sharing images – sRGB, the web's default;

faq.which.li2.t: designing palettes and gradients – OKLCH, where equal steps look equal;

faq.which.li3.t: math on light (blending, blurring, 3D) – linear-light RGB;

faq.which.li4.t: shooting and grading video – your camera's log space, delivered in Rec. 709 or Rec. 2100;

faq.which.li5.t: measuring how different two colors look – CIELAB or DIN99o.

faq.which.p2.t: To see every space sorted by task, group the catalog by purpose.

faq.which.q.t: Which space should I actually use?

lore.a98rgb.for.t: a Photoshop working space reaching printable cyans and greens

lore.a98rgb.sin.t: born of a bug – an engineer transcribed SMPTE 240M primaries wrong, and the accident shipped

lore.aces2-jmh.for.t: tone-map and gamut-map ACES images for a display while holding each color’s hue

lore.aces2-jmh.nm.t: J lightness, M colorfulness, h hue – the appearance-model letters; 2 for ACES 2.0

lore.aces2-jmh.sin.t: not a general appearance model: viewing conditions are fixed and colorfulness drops Hellwig’s eccentricity factor

lore.aces2065-1.for.t: the archival master – AP0 primaries wrap everything visible

lore.aces2065-1.nm.t: named for its SMPTE standard number, ST 2065-1

lore.aces2065-1.sin.t: AP0 is mostly imaginary: great vault, terrible working space

lore.acescc.for.t: pure-log grading space – dials feel like film printer lights

lore.acescc.sin.t: pure log has no toe: near-black codes get twitchy

lore.acescct.for.t: ACEScc with a toe, so lifted blacks grade like film

lore.acescct.nm.t: the extra t is the toe

lore.acescg.for.t: the render/compositing space of the ACES pipeline – linear, wide but real

lore.acescg.nm.t: CG = computer graphics; primaries called AP1

lore.acesproxy.for.t: on-set monitoring log – integer-friendly, never stored

lore.adx10.for.t: film scans in one defined printing density, whatever the scanner, so a single Academy transform takes them into ACES

lore.adx10.nm.t: Academy Density Exchange; 10 for its 10-bit codes

lore.adx10.sin.t: 10 bits stop at 1.856 of red density above the base – ST 2065-3 itself notes some negative and internegative stocks exceed it

lore.adx16.for.t: the full ADX range and precision – the form ST 2065-3 tells you to use whenever you can

lore.adx16.nm.t: Academy Density Exchange; 16 for its 16-bit codes

lore.anlab.for.t: chromatic-valence ΔE for textiles – the direct ancestor of CIELAB

lore.apple-rgb.for.t: the classic Mac Trinitron display, frozen as a profile

lore.applelog.for.t: ProRes Log on iPhone 15 Pro – a phone speaking cinema

lore.applelog2.for.t: Apple Log off the BT.2020 container – the same curve on primaries tuned to iPhone sensors

lore.atd95.for.t: the opponent pathway itself – discrimination and adaptation, not just appearance

lore.awg3.for.t: one fixed camera RGB for ALEXA footage, so VFX can invert Log C to scene linear and convert with a single matrix

lore.awg3.nm.t: formerly ALEXA Wide Gamut RGB; 3 = ARRI’s third color-science generation

lore.awg4.for.t: the ALEXA 35’s gamut, defined within ACES AP0 alongside LogC4

lore.awg4.sin.t: CAT02-adapted into an ACES AP0 container, its outer edge can still go negative (ARRI’s own spec warns of it)

lore.bestrgb.for.t: Don RGB 4 widened to hold Fujichrome Velvia’s saturated reds and magentas

lore.bestrgb.sin.t: its blue lies just outside the spectral locus – about 3.5% of code values encode no real color

lore.betargb.for.t: the smallest RGB gamut that holds a reference set of film, chart and printing colors

lore.betargb.sin.t: 10- and 12-ink pigment inkjets exceed it in the cyans and blues – the reason Russell RGB exists

lore.bmdwg.for.t: the camera gamut of Blackmagic’s Gen 5 color science, decoded from Blackmagic RAW

lore.bmdwg.nm.t: BMD = Blackmagic Design; Gen 5 = its fifth color-science generation

lore.bmdwg.sin.t: its white is published as D65 to seven digits (0.3127170, 0.3290312), so tools that keep it and tools that use 4-digit D65 disagree by up to ~2.5e-4

lore.brucergb.for.t: a safe 8-bit editing space between ColorMatch RGB’s cyan clipping and Adobe RGB (1998)’s unprintable excess

lore.brucergb.nm.t: named after its author, Bruce Fraser

lore.brucergb.sin.t: clips fully saturated yellows about as much as Adobe RGB (1998)

lore.cam02-ucs.for.t: CIECAM02 as a uniform space – the ΔE workhorse of the 2010s

lore.cam16-lcd.for.t: the variant tuned for large differences

lore.cam16-scd.for.t: the variant tuned for small differences

lore.cam16-ucs.for.t: CAM16 squeezed into a uniform space – modern ΔE work

lore.cam16.for.t: fix CIECAM02’s numerical failures with one cleaner adaptation transform

lore.cam16.nm.t: CAM = colour appearance model; 16 is 2016 – the CIE adopted it, as CIECAM16, in 2022

lore.cam16.sin.t: a full viewing-conditions model: powerful, and overkill anywhere conditions are unknown

lore.cct-duv.for.t: specifying white light with both warm–cool temperature and green–pink tint

lore.cct-duv.nm.t: correlated color temperature plus signed distance in CIE 1960 uv

lore.cct-duv.sin.t: meaningful only near the Planckian locus; it discards luminance

lore.cie-rgb.for.t: the primaries of the Wright–Guild experiments that defined the standard observer

lore.cie-rgb.sin.t: needs negative red to match spectral cyans – the very problem XYZ was invented to hide

lore.ciecam02.for.t: the committee appearance model behind Windows Color System

lore.ciecam02.nm.t: CAM = colour appearance model; 02 is the year, 2002

lore.ciecam02.sin.t: its CAT02 matrix can go negative for saturated blues – the defect that begat CAM16

lore.ciecam16.for.t: the CIE’s 2022 replacement for CIECAM02 in color management: CAM16 with straight-line ends on its response compression

lore.ciecam16.nm.t: the report’s title calls it “the CIE 2016 colour appearance model”; it was published as CIE 248:2022

lore.ciecam97s.for.t: one appearance model the imaging industry could share, asked of the CIE at its 1996 Vienna symposium

lore.ciecam97s.nm.t: s is “simple version”; the report promised a comprehensive CIECAM97c

lore.ciecam97s.sin.t: black sits at lightness J ≈ 2.2, not 0, and the report’s own inverse is only approximate

lore.cineon.for.t: film scans as printing density – the grandfather of every camera log

lore.cineon.nm.t: named for Kodak’s Cineon digital film system of the early 1990s

lore.clog.nm.t: C is Canon – a different “C” from ARRI’s Log C, where C is for Cineon

lore.clog2.for.t: the grading log for maximum dynamic range

lore.clog3.for.t: the in-between: more range than C-Log, friendlier than C-Log2

lore.cmy.for.t: subtractive mixing at its simplest – the teaching model

lore.cmyk.for.t: process printing’s four plates as a space

lore.cmyk.nm.t: K is the key plate – the one others register to – not “blacK”

lore.cmyk.sin.t: the naive formula: real separation needs ICC profiles, ink limits and black generation

lore.colormatch.for.t: matching Radius PressView calibrated monitors in professional graphic arts

lore.colormatch.sin.t: clips printable cyans and the blues and greens next to them (Fraser, 2000)

lore.coloroid.for.t: aesthetic spacing for architects – harmony intervals, not ΔE

lore.coloroid.nm.t: A, T, V: árnyalat, telítettség, világosság – hue, saturation, lightness in Hungarian

lore.cubehelix.for.t: colormaps for astronomical images whose NTSC luma rises steadily from black to white, so they stay ordered in grayscale

lore.cubehelix.nm.t: a squashed helix around the gray diagonal of the RGB cube – Green’s “cube helix”

lore.cubehelix.sin.t: L is luma on gamma-encoded RGB, not perceived lightness – Green warns printed versions may not look monotonic

lore.davinci.for.t: DaVinci Wide Gamut Intermediate – one grading space for any camera

lore.davinci.nm.t: named for DaVinci Resolve, Blackmagic’s own grading software

lore.dcdm.for.t: the projector’s master format: XYZ with a 2.6 gamma

lore.dci-p3-plus.for.t: more saturated color than DCI-P3 from the Canon EOS C500, keeping the DCI white

lore.dci-p3-plus.sin.t: its blue primary has y = −0.09 – outside the visible gamut, so part of the code range is imaginary

lore.dci-p3.for.t: a gamut real xenon projectors could cover

lore.dci-p3.sin.t: its native white is greenish ~6300 K cinema white, not D65 – grading for TV needs adaptation

lore.dgamut.for.t: DJI’s cinema gamut, covering Rec.709 and DCI-P3 with primaries aligned to P3’s so hues hold in gamut mapping

lore.dgamut.sin.t: its published matrix has 4 decimals, so RGB white lands 6e-5 off D65

lore.din99.for.t: a Euclidean stand-in for CIE94: plain distance in the space tracks ΔE94, no weighting functions

lore.din99.sin.t: blue tolerance ellipses stay elongated – the defect the 2002 b/c/d revisions set out to fix

lore.din99c.for.t: DIN99 with the blue fixed: a share of Z mixed into X before CIELAB rounds the blue tolerance ellipses

lore.din99c.nm.t: “c” is sequential – the second of the 2002 revisions b, c, d

lore.din99d.for.t: the DIN99 revision tuned for small differences

lore.din99d.nm.t: “d” is sequential – the third of the 2002 revisions b, c, d

lore.din99o-lab.for.t: warp Lab so plain Euclidean distance works as ΔE

lore.din99o-lab.nm.t: “99” is the year, “o” the optimized revision

lore.dkl.for.t: the axes LGN neurons actually respond to – cone-opponent, isoluminant

lore.dlog.nm.t: D is DJI – distinct from D-Log M, the separate curve on DJI’s consumer drones

lore.donrgb4.for.t: holding the Ektachrome film gamut with virtually no clipping

lore.donrgb4.nm.t: Don Hutcheson’s fourth trial version, named in 1996 by Apple ColorSync product manager Damon Rando

lore.dsh.for.t: colorimetry’s classic triple: dominant wavelength, saturation, brightness – Helmholtz coordinates

lore.dsh.sin.t: purples have no dominant wavelength, only a complementary one – the space folds there

lore.dwg.for.t: one wide gamut DaVinci Resolve converts every camera into before grading

lore.dwg.nm.t: named for DaVinci Resolve, Blackmagic’s grading software

lore.dwg.sin.t: its whitepaper shipped wrong matrix values and a wrong green x, fixed in v1.0.1 (2020) and v1.1 (2021)

lore.ecirgb.for.t: print-oriented RGB for European prepress, encoded so equal code steps are equal L* steps

lore.ecirgb.nm.t: ECI = European Color Initiative; v2 (2007) replaced v1’s gamma 1.8 with the L* curve

lore.egamut.for.t: FilmLight’s camera-agnostic working gamut under T-Log in Baselight

lore.erimm.nm.t: ER = extended range, stretching RIMM’s headroom

lore.filmicpro.for.t: the app log that made phones gradeable

lore.flog.nm.t: F is Fujifilm; F-Gamut, its matching primaries, shares BT.2020 chromaticities

lore.flog2c.for.t: F-Log2 with room for more saturated color – the same curve, on a gamut that encloses BT.2020

lore.flog2c.nm.t: the F-Log2 curve recorded on F-Gamut C

lore.gplog2.for.t: pure-log capture on GoPro’s MISSION 1 series – log base 600, clipping about 1.8 stops above white

lore.gplog2.sin.t: GoPro’s docs quote clip-relative linear (18% grey = 0.0517); scene linear here is 2^1.8 larger – the LUT generator’s default +1.8 EV – so mixing the two shifts exposure by 1.8 stops

lore.hcg.for.t: HSV refactored as chroma plus gray base

lore.hcl.for.t: hue–chroma–luminance picker math (not the Lab-based LCh)

lore.hct.for.t: dynamic theming: pick tone for contrast, keep hue and chroma honest

lore.hct.sin.t: two models stitched together – CAM16 hue/chroma with Lab tone – so the inverse needs a solver

lore.hcy.nm.t: hue, chroma, luma – Y is Rec.601 luma, not lightness

lore.hdr-cie-lab.for.t: Lab rebuilt for HDR – the cube root swapped for a luminance-aware curve

lore.hdr-ipt.for.t: IPT rebuilt for HDR luminance ranges

lore.hellwig2022-hk.for.t: make saturated colors read as light as they look – the Helmholtz–Kohlrausch effect

lore.hellwig2022-hk.nm.t: HK = Helmholtz–Kohlrausch, the effect it adds to Hellwig 2022’s lightness

lore.hellwig2022.for.t: CAM16 pruned to what vision data actually supports

lore.hellwig2022.nm.t: named for its authors, Hellwig & Fairchild, and their 2022 paper

lore.helmgen.for.t: Oklab-style gradients without the dark-end cusps or purple blue-to-white midpoints

lore.helmgen.nm.t: Helmlab’s generation space (GenSpace); its sibling MetricSpace is for ΔE

lore.helmgen.sin.t: refit between releases – v0.10’s softened cube root became v0.11’s depressed cubic – so coordinates depend on the version

lore.helmgenlch.for.t: the polar form of HelmGen, for hue-led ramps

lore.helmlab-metric.for.t: predicting how different two colors look – one space and its ΔE fit together to 3,813 judged pairs

lore.helmlab-metric.nm.t: Helmlab’s measuring space (MetricSpace); its sibling HelmGen is for generation

lore.helmlab-metric.sin.t: by its author’s own count it trails CIEDE2000 on He et al. 2022’s 82 3D-printed pairs (STRESS 35.9 vs 32.6)

lore.hpluv.for.t: the pastel variant – chroma capped so every hue can reach it

lore.hpluv.sin.t: only pastels: the cap is the dullest hue’s maximum

lore.hsi.for.t: machine-vision variant where I is the plain mean of R,G,B

lore.hsi.sin.t: hue is numerically unstable near gray – sensor noise sends it spinning

lore.hsl.for.t: hue controls cheap enough for 1970s framebuffers

lore.hsl.nm.t: lightness – the double-cone: L=100 is always white

lore.hsl.sin.t: L=50 is not one brightness: yellow at L=50 emits ~13× the luminance of blue

lore.hsluv.for.t: an HSL that never lies about lightness – L is CIE L*, saturation is share of the possible chroma

lore.hsm.for.t: hue–saturation–mixture, built for skin segmentation research

lore.hsp.for.t: HSV with a brightness much closer to the eye’s

lore.hsp.nm.t: P = perceived brightness, a weighted RMS of R,G,B

lore.hsv.for.t: painter-style “tints and shades” for early paint programs

lore.hsv.nm.t: aka HSB; V=100 is the pure hue, not white

lore.hsv.sin.t: V is just max(R,G,B): full-value blue and yellow claim equal brightness and are nowhere near

lore.hunt.for.t: the whole appearance picture – rods included – from starlight to bright daylight

lore.hunt.nm.t: named for Robert Hunt, who built it over three decades at Kodak

lore.hunt.sin.t: so many viewing-condition parameters that two faithful implementations rarely agree

lore.hunter-rdab.for.t: reflectance plus opponent readings that 1940s analog colorimeters could compute from X, Y, Z

lore.hunter-rdab.sin.t: a and b shrink as Rd falls toward black; the empirical f(Y) factor only slows the collapse

lore.hwb.for.t: mixing the way painters think – a hue plus white plus black

lore.hwb.sin.t: W+B>100 produces gray; hue no longer affects the result

lore.iapbp.for.t: a uniform HDR/WCG space with low lightness–chroma crosstalk for image processing

lore.iapbp.sin.t: no published inverse, code or worked example, and its reference white’s luminance is never stated

lore.icacb.for.t: an HDR ΔE space in the ICtCp family

lore.icacb.nm.t: I intensity, Ca red-green, Cb yellow-blue – ICtCp’s layout with Lab-style axis letters

lore.ictcp-hlg.for.t: ICtCp’s constant-intensity chroma for HLG chains

lore.ictcp-hlg.nm.t: I intensity, Ct tritan, Cp protan; HLG = Hybrid Log-Gamma

lore.ictcp-hlg.sin.t: BT.2100 keeps Y′C′bC′r the default; ICtCp is for exchange only by mutual agreement

lore.ictcp.for.t: HDR grading axes that keep luminance out of chroma, PQ-encoded

lore.ictcp.nm.t: I intensity, Ct tritan (blue–yellow), Cp protan (red–green)

lore.igpgtg.for.t: an IPT-style space refit to the hues of Gaussian spectra instead of visual data

lore.igpgtg.nm.t: g-subscripted I/P/T – intensity, protan, tritan, as in IPT

lore.ihls.for.t: image analysis – a saturation that stays near zero for every near-gray and ignores brightness, so hue statistics can be weighted by it

lore.ihls.nm.t: Improved HLS – Y is Rec. 709 luma, S is max − min

lore.ilog.for.t: wide-range capture from 360 and gimbal cameras that drops into a cinema grading pipeline

lore.ilog.sin.t: one name, more than one curve – its white paper logs a new transfer function in July 2025, so a decode is only right against the curve the footage was shot with

lore.ipt-ragoo.for.t: IPT refit to trade hue linearity against uniformity

lore.ipt-ragoo.nm.t: IPT plus its first author, Ragoo (Ragoo & Farup 2021)

lore.ipt-ragoo.sin.t: trained and tested on the same data sets, as the authors note

lore.ipt.for.t: straight constant-hue lines – gamut mapping without hue drift

lore.ipt.nm.t: I intensity, P protan, T tritan

lore.iptpqc2.for.t: Dolby Vision profile 5 delivery: IPT with PQ-coded cones

lore.iptpqc2.nm.t: IPT, PQ transfer, C2 = 2 % cone crosstalk

lore.iptpqc2.sin.t: consumer distribution only (ST 2128); real profile 5 streams also need the RPU reshaping metadata

lore.jpeg.for.t: full-range YCbCr as the still-image workhorse

lore.jzazbz.for.t: a Lab that stays uniform to 10,000 nits

lore.jzazbz.nm.t: Lab’s letters in PQ dress – Jz, az, bz

lore.jzazbz.sin.t: built on PQ: values depend on absolute luminance, so SDR use needs a brightness assumption

lore.kelvin.for.t: the color of a glowing blackbody as a one-dial space

lore.kelvin.nm.t: after Lord Kelvin’s absolute temperature scale

lore.kelvin.sin.t: only the Planckian locus exists – every real white needs a tint offset the scale cannot say

lore.kim2009.for.t: appearance across extended luminance, measured up to 16,860 cd/m², for HDR tone mapping

lore.kim2009.nm.t: named for its authors, Kim, Weyrich & Kautz, and their 2009 SIGGRAPH paper

lore.kim2009.sin.t: lightness turns negative for dark colors: black sits near J −108 on the CRT media setting

lore.kinelog3.for.t: Kinefinity’s film-scan-style camera log, on the wide gamut of the MAVO Edge 6K and MM2 LF

lore.kinelog3.sin.t: an earlier copy of its spec, same date, prints blue y −0.2282 with matrices that disagree – the revised −0.2236 is the one that holds together

lore.lab-d65.for.t: Lab referenced to D65 – display work without the D50 detour

lore.lab.for.t: make color difference measurable – one number, ΔE, for “how far apart”

lore.lab.nm.t: the * in L*a*b* set it apart from Hunter’s 1958 Lab

lore.lab.sin.t: constant-hue lines bend in blue: Lab gradients drift toward purple

lore.labh.for.t: uniform-ish readings straight from photoelectric colorimeters – square roots, no cube roots

lore.labh.nm.t: the starless Lab – CIE added the * in 1976 to avoid the collision

lore.labh.sin.t: superseded by CIELAB everywhere except a few industry standards and legacy instruments

lore.lalphabeta.for.t: the statistics of natural scenes, decorrelated – the engine of Reinhard color transfer

lore.lchab.for.t: Lab in polar form – chroma and hue as dials

lore.lchuv.nm.t: LCh(uv): C=√(u²+v²), h=atan2(v,u) – polar Luv, as LCh(ab) is polar Lab

lore.llab.for.t: cross-media reproduction – a CIELAB successor that survives a change of surround and medium

lore.lms.for.t: the cones themselves – long, medium, short – where chromatic adaptation actually happens

lore.log3g10.nm.t: log; 3 – mid-gray encodes at 1/3; G10 – 10 stops above mid-gray reach 1.0

lore.logc3.for.t: ALEXA’s scene-referred log – exposure stops spaced evenly

lore.logc3.nm.t: Log C: C for Cineon lineage; v3 is the EI-dependent family

lore.logluv.for.t: HDR images in TIFF – 38 orders of magnitude in 0.27% steps and the full visible gamut in 32 bits per pixel

lore.logluv.nm.t: log luminance plus CIE 1976 u′v′ – Luv’s chromaticity, not CIELUV’s L*

lore.logluv.sin.t: absolute cd/m² only when the file carries a STONITS tag – often it does not

lore.lrgb.for.t: the linear-light form – where physical math (blending, shading, resampling) is correct

lore.lrgb.sin.t: perceptually lopsided: three quarters of its numeric range covers the brightest stops

lore.luv.for.t: the additive-light sibling of Lab – chromaticity stays projective, so light mixtures travel in straight lines

lore.luv.nm.t: u,v come from the 1960 uniform chromaticity diagram

lore.luv.sin.t: good for lights, worse for surfaces – print went Lab, lighting went Luv

lore.macboyn.for.t: chromaticity in cone space – vision science’s working diagram

lore.maxwell.for.t: plotting three receptor catches as chromaticity – the comparative-vision triangle

lore.maxwell.nm.t: named for James Clerk Maxwell, whose 1860 colour triangle it generalizes

lore.msh.for.t: diverging color maps that pass through a smooth white center instead of a Mach band

lore.msh.nm.t: M magnitude, s saturation, h hue – the Lab vector in spherical coordinates

lore.msh.sin.t: a pole on the L* axis: at s = 0 hue is undefined, so a map through white needs a hue-spin rule

lore.munsell.for.t: the first perceptual order system – steps an art student can trust

lore.munsell.nm.t: his words “value” and “chroma” are still the field’s vocabulary

lore.munsell.sin.t: defined by the 1943 renotation tables: a lookup with interpolation, not a formula

lore.nayatani95.for.t: what rising illuminance itself does to colour – the Hunt and Stevens effects, modelled head-on

lore.nlog.for.t: Nikon’s log for the Z line

lore.nlog.nm.t: N is Nikon; N-Gamut, its matching primaries, shares BT.2020 chromaticities

lore.ntsc.sin.t: no consumer set ever matched its phosphors – it survives mainly as a marketing benchmark (“72% NTSC”)

lore.ohta.for.t: segmentation channels that decorrelate natural images with integer-cheap math

lore.ohta.nm.t: I1I2I3 in the paper – named for its first author here

lore.okhsl.for.t: an HSL whose lightness and hue track perception, mapped to the sRGB gamut

lore.okhsl.sin.t: sRGB-bound by construction – there is no wide-gamut okhsl

lore.okhsv.for.t: the HSV counterpart – perceptual tints and shades inside sRGB

lore.okhwb.for.t: HWB’s white/black mixing lifted onto the okhsv machinery

lore.oklab.for.t: Lab’s job without Lab’s blue drift – fitted to CAM16 data, cheap enough for a shader

lore.oklab.nm.t: “OK” is literal: named for doing an OK job

lore.oklab.sin.t: tuned for D65 display work – it has no viewing-conditions story at all, by design

lore.oklch.for.t: the polar form CSS adopted – perceptual hue and chroma as dials

lore.oklch.nm.t: lightness, chroma, hue – OKLab in polar form

lore.oklrab.for.t: OKLab with Lr – lightness given a toe so mid-grays sit where displays put them

lore.oklrch.nm.t: Lr (toe-corrected lightness), chroma, hue – OKLrab in polar form

lore.olog2.for.t: OPPO’s second phone log: one base-2 log curve on BT.2020, shipped with LUTs and an ACES transform

lore.olog2.nm.t: O for OPPO; 2 = its second log profile

lore.olog2.sin.t: OPPO publishes no white paper for it; the 4-digit constants in its ACES CTL are the only definition

lore.orgb.for.t: Hering opponent axes, yellow–blue and red–green, computed straight from R′G′B′ for graphics tasks like color adjustment and color transfer

lore.orgb.nm.t: o for opponent – L′ luma, Cyb yellow–blue, Crg red–green

lore.orgb.sin.t: the hue remap is piecewise linear in angle – slope 3/2 below 60°, 3/4 above – so hue spacing kinks at the seam

lore.osaucs-ee.for.t: a color-difference formula that is plain distance, not built on CIELAB – as good as CIEDE2000 on many visual datasets

lore.osaucs-ee.nm.t: L_E, G_E, J_E: OSA-UCS lightness, greenness and yellowness after log compression; ΔE_E is their distance

lore.osaucs-ee.sin.t: fitted to small and medium differences only – for large steps the uncompressed OSA-UCS is the scale

lore.osaucs.for.t: the most uniform lattice ever measured – thirty years of committee judgments

lore.osaucs.nm.t: L, j, g: j is yellowness (jaune), g greenness

lore.osaucs.sin.t: no closed-form inverse, and its √2 lattice neighbors make it a dataset more than a picker

lore.ostwald.for.t: colour ordered the way a painter mixes it – one full colour cut with white and black

lore.ostwald.nm.t: named for Wilhelm Ostwald, the Nobel chemist who systematised it

lore.ostwald.sin.t: its “full colours” are ideal semichromes: no ink or display reaches them, so the outer shell is unreachable

lore.p3.for.t: DCI cinema primaries domesticated for displays – D65 white, sRGB curve

lore.p3.nm.t: Display P3 – the P3 gamut minus the projector

lore.photoycc.for.t: PhotoCD’s scene-referred YCC – film scans with highlight headroom

lore.poirson-wandell.for.t: the opponent channels S-CIELAB blurs, each with its own spatial sensitivity, before converting to CIELAB

lore.poirson-wandell.nm.t: named for Allen Poirson and Brian Wandell; Johnson & Fairchild write its channels A, C1, C2

lore.poirson-wandell.sin.t: not white-normalized: D65 sits at O2 −5.3, O3 3.7, so zero chroma is not neutral

lore.prismatic.for.t: quick hue and saturation edits in an iPhone photo app (Subjective): hue as the Maxwell triangle, lightness as max(R,G,B)

lore.prismatic.nm.t: every cross-section is the same triangle, so the color volume is a prism

lore.prismatic.sin.t: L = max(R,G,B) is not lightness – pure blue and white both read L = 1

lore.prolab.for.t: a projective transform of XYZ that stays perceptually even – angles survive illumination change

lore.prolab.nm.t: pro = projective: a single projective transform of XYZ, not Lab’s per-channel cube root

lore.prophoto.for.t: room for everything film and future printers could hold

lore.prophoto.nm.t: standardized as ROMM RGB (Reference Output Medium Metric)

lore.prophoto.sin.t: two primaries are imaginary – ~13% of its volume is no color at all, and 8-bit files band visibly

lore.ral-design.for.t: industrial coatings organized by CIELAB hue–lightness–chroma

lore.ral-design.nm.t: each code reads H, L, C

lore.rec2020-display.for.t: CSS’s color(rec2020 …): BT.2020 primaries under the BT.1886 2.4 power

lore.rec2020-display.nm.t: display: the reference display’s decoding – what CSS writes as color(rec2020 …)

lore.rec2020-display.sin.t: rec2020 can mean two curves: decoding with the inverse BT.2020 camera curve instead (colorjs.io 0.5 did) gives signal 0.5 37 % more light

lore.rec2020-linear.for.t: Rec.2020 in linear light, for compositing math

lore.rec2020.sin.t: primaries are pure laser wavelengths – no consumer display fully covers it, so most Rec.2020 content is smaller than its box

lore.rec2100-hlg.for.t: HDR that still looks right on SDR sets – broadcast’s one-signal answer

lore.rec2100-hlg.nm.t: hybrid log-gamma: gamma toe, logarithmic shoulder

lore.rec2100-pq.for.t: absolute HDR signals – code steps sized to the eye’s contrast threshold

lore.rec709-display.for.t: what a BT.1886 studio monitor emits for Rec. 709 code values – the decoding BT.709 itself points to

lore.rec709-display.nm.t: display: decoded as the reference monitor shows it, not as the camera encoded it

lore.rec709-display.sin.t: black fixed at zero: BT.1886 lifts the curve by the monitor’s measured black (its b term), so a real panel shows near-black steps lighter than this

lore.rec709.for.t: the HDTV standard – sRGB later borrowed its primaries

lore.rg.for.t: normalized rg chromaticity – brightness divided out for illumination-robust vision

lore.rgb-display.for.t: what a monitor calibrated to a pure 2.2 power shows for sRGB values

lore.rgb-display.nm.t: display: the reference display’s 2.2 power, not the piecewise encoding

lore.rgb-display.sin.t: the sRGB display curve is disputed: IEC 61966-2-1 names a 2.2 reference display, the ICC reads 2.2 as approximate and the piecewise curve as exact; the two part in the shadows (0.63 % against 1.00 % of white at signal 0.1)

lore.rgb.for.t: Default for monitors, printers and web – the average CRT, standardized

lore.rgb.sin.t: gamma-encoded: averaging two colors numerically gives a darker color than mixing their light

lore.rimm.for.t: the scene-referred sibling of ROMM – camera light before rendering

lore.rlab.for.t: Lab with adaptation done right, sized for imaging work

lore.russellrgb.for.t: Beta RGB widened into the cyans and blues to hold 10- and 12-ink pigment inkjet gamuts

lore.russellrgb.nm.t: named after its author, Russell Cottrell

lore.rwg.for.t: a standardized RED camera RGB that holds every color a RED sensor can produce without clipping

lore.rwg.nm.t: RWG for short, RED’s own abbreviation

lore.rwg.sin.t: its green primary sits at y ≈ 1.49, so much of its code volume encodes no real color

lore.ryb.for.t: the painter’s wheel every kindergarten teaches

lore.ryb.sin.t: no standard exists – every RYB implementation mixes differently

lore.samsunglog.for.t: Galaxy phone video kept for post – wide dynamic range and room to rework color and contrast

lore.scam.for.t: CAM16-style lightness, colorfulness and hue from a short pipeline built on sUCS

lore.scam.nm.t: s is “simple”: “Simple color appearance model (sCAM)”, Li & Luo’s 2024 title

lore.scrgb.for.t: sRGB with headroom – negatives and >1 allowed for HDR compositing on Windows

lore.scrgb.sin.t: most software clips its out-of-range values on sight

lore.sgamut3-venice.for.t: Venice footage in ACES – Sony’s own Venice matrix in place of the generic S-Gamut3 one

lore.sgamut3-venice.sin.t: Sony published only the matrix to ACES: the primaries are a derivation that assumes a D65 white and CAT02

lore.sgamut3.for.t: Sony’s wide camera gamut under S-Log3, keeping the original S-Gamut primaries

lore.sgamut3cine-venice.for.t: Venice’s S-Gamut3.Cine footage in ACES – Sony’s own Venice matrix in place of the generic S-Gamut3.Cine one

lore.sgamut3cine-venice.sin.t: Sony published only the matrix to ACES: the primaries are a derivation that assumes a D65 white and CAT02

lore.sgamut3cine.for.t: S-Gamut3 pulled in toward DCI-P3, so Sony footage grades straight to a cinema target

lore.sgamut3cine.nm.t: Sony’s S-Gamut, third revision; “.Cine” is the DCI-P3-leaning variant

lore.slog.nm.t: S is Sony – paired with its own S-Gamut primaries

lore.slog2.for.t: log for the F65, F55 and F5 generation

lore.slog3.for.t: the Cineon-like revision most Sony cine cameras speak today

lore.smpte-240m.sin.t: remembered mostly because misreading its numbers created Adobe RGB

lore.smpte-c.for.t: the phosphors US broadcast actually used, standardized after the fact

lore.srlab2.for.t: CIELAB’s structure with OSA-grade hue uniformity, kept invertible

lore.sucs.for.t: a lightweight uniform color space, the base of the sCAM appearance model

lore.sucs.nm.t: s is “simple” – the uniform space Li & Luo built their sCAM appearance model on

lore.tlog.for.t: FilmLight’s Baselight-native log on E-Gamut – a camera-agnostic grading intermediate

lore.tlog.nm.t: T for Truelight, FilmLight’s colour pipeline

lore.tsl.for.t: skin detection – chromaticity warped so faces cluster tightly

lore.ucs.for.t: a chromaticity diagram where distance means something

lore.ucs.sin.t: obsolete – it survives only inside correlated color temperature math

lore.uv.for.t: the chromaticity plane color-shift tolerances (Δu′v′) are measured in

lore.uv.nm.t: u,v – later refined to u′,v′ in 1976

lore.uvw.for.t: the first CIE uniform 3-D space, built for color rendering index

lore.uvw.sin.t: obsolete – CRI is the only place you will meet it

lore.vgamut.for.t: a master-archive gamut for VARICAM 35 footage, reached by tuning the sensor’s on-chip color filters

lore.viperlog.for.t: the Viper FilmStream camera – raw log that helped start digital cinema

lore.vlog.for.t: VariCam’s log, one curve across sensors

lore.vlog.nm.t: V is for VariCam, the camera it launched on

lore.wavelength.for.t: the spectral colors as a line – the horseshoe’s rim by nanometer

lore.wavelength.sin.t: no purples: the line between violet and red is not in it

lore.widegamut.for.t: a Photoshop working space on spectral primaries, wide enough for saturated film and print colors

lore.widegamut.sin.t: about 8% of its code values are colors that do not exist; 8-bit files band, so 16-bit editing is recommended

lore.xvycc.for.t: extended-gamut video smuggled through BT.709 negatives

lore.xvycc.nm.t: IEC 61966-2-4’s title – “extended-gamut YCC colour space for video applications”

lore.xyb.for.t: the codec’s cone-based space – built to hide compression error, not to look at

lore.xyb.nm.t: X ≈ L−M opponent; Y luminance-ish; B for blue (S-cone), stored as B − Y

lore.xyy.for.t: chromaticity split from luminance – the space the horseshoe diagram lives in

lore.xyy.sin.t: perceptually non-uniform: MacAdam’s ellipses vary 80× across it

lore.xyz-abs-d65.for.t: XYZ carrying absolute luminance in cd/m², for HDR math

lore.xyz-d50.for.t: XYZ adapted to D50 – the ICC profile connection space

lore.xyz.for.t: one standard observer for all eyes – color reduced to three integrals

lore.xyz.nm.t: chosen so Y alone is luminance; X and Z carry the rest without negative lobes

lore.xyz.sin.t: imaginary primaries on purpose: nothing you can see sits at X, Y or Z itself

lore.ycbcr-bt601-525.for.t: 525-line SD legal-range video with SMPTE-C primaries

lore.ycbcr-bt601-625.for.t: 625-line SD legal-range video with PAL/EBU primaries

lore.ycbcr.for.t: squeeze color into less bandwidth than luma – the eye forgives chroma blur

lore.ycbcr.nm.t: the prime on Y′ matters – luma, not luminance

lore.ycbcr.sin.t: older variant with adjustable parameters; when the signal standard is known, choose the matching BT.601/709/2020 variant

lore.yccbccrc.for.t: the constant-luminance YCbCr of BT.2020 – BT.2100 left it out

lore.ycgco.for.t: a lossless, lifting-friendly transform for codecs – two adds and two shifts

lore.ycgco.nm.t: Cg green difference, Co orange difference

lore.ycxcz.for.t: filtering color images in linear light along CIELAB-aligned axes – halftone design and blur-based difference metrics such as NVIDIA’s FLIP

lore.ycxcz.nm.t: Yy: Y scaled like L*; Cx and Cz: X − Y and Y − Z, scaled like a* and b* without the cube root

lore.ycxcz.sin.t: linear in XYZ, so not perceptually uniform: measure differences only after converting to CIELAB

lore.ydbdr.for.t: the French answer – color differences sent one per line

lore.ydzdx.for.t: luma plus color-difference coding of PQ-encoded X′Y′Z′, signalled in video as H.273 matrix coefficients 11

lore.ydzdx.sin.t: the weights null D65 only at 500 cd/m² – PQ curvature leaves neutrals slightly off zero at other levels

lore.yes.for.t: a luma plus two chroma axes used in early face-detection work

lore.yes.nm.t: Y luminance, E green-red, S blue-yellow chrominance

lore.yiq.for.t: bandwidth shaped to the eye: I gets 1.3 MHz, Q gets 0.4, because orange–cyan acuity beats green–purple

lore.yiq.nm.t: in-phase and quadrature of the color subcarrier

lore.ypbpr.for.t: analog component video – the three-cable YCbCr

lore.yuv.for.t: hide color inside a black-and-white-compatible signal

lore.yuv.nm.t: U,V – the analog scaling of B−Y and R−Y

lore.zcam.for.t: an appearance model born HDR – PQ-based like Jzazbz

space.a98rgb-linear.desc.t: Linear-light Adobe RGB — Adobe RGB (1998) without its gamma curve: the same wider-than-sRGB primaries and D65 white, with channel values proportional to light intensity.

space.a98rgb-linear.use.t: Color math on Adobe RGB values, before re-encoding to its gamma curve.

space.a98rgb.desc.t: Adobe RGB — Adobe's 1998 wider-gamut alternative to sRGB, made to reach more of the cyans and greens that CMYK printing can reproduce. It keeps sRGB's D65 white but uses different primaries and a slightly different gamma.

space.a98rgb.use.t: Photography and print, where sRGB's gamut clips CMYK-reproducible colors.

space.aces2-jmh.desc.t: ACES 2.0 JMh is the appearance space the ACES 2.0 output transforms work in. They convert ACES2065-1 to lightness J, colorfulness M and hue h, tone-map J and compress M at constant hue, then convert to the display's RGB. The model is a simplified Hellwig 2022: viewing conditions fixed at a 100 cd/m² reference white and adapting field, background Y_b 20 and a dim surround, full adaptation to the ACES white, a cone matrix built from its own primaries in place of CAT16, and no eccentricity factor in colorfulness.

space.aces2-jmh.use.t: The working space of the ACES 2.0 output transforms, where tone scale, chroma compression and gamut compression run; OpenColorIO exposes it as the fixed function ACES_RGB_TO_JMh_20.

space.aces2065-1.desc.t: ACES2065-1 — the Academy Color Encoding System's archival and interchange master format, on AP0 primaries that enclose the whole visible gamut, with a white near D60. Like ACEScg, it stores scene-referred light linearly, with values far past nominal white to keep highlight detail for later grading or rendering. AMPAS made it the long-term, camera-agnostic exchange format for finished masters; day-to-day rendering uses ACEScg's smaller AP1 gamut.

space.aces2065-1.use.t: Archiving and exchanging finished ACES film and TV masters.

space.acescc.desc.t: ACEScc is a logarithmic ACES space for color grading, with the same AP1 primaries as ACEScg. Its curve is based on log2 and, unlike ACEScct, has no linear segment near black. After grading, footage is converted back to ACEScg or ACES2065-1 for the final render.

space.acescc.use.t: Log2 color-grading space in ACES post-production; on legacy control surfaces largely superseded by ACEScct.

space.acescct.desc.t: ACEScct is an ACES space for color grading. It uses ACEScg's AP1 primaries and ACEScc's log2 curve, with an added linear segment near black. This segment adjusts the response of shadows to lift/gamma/gain controls to suit traditional grading tools.

space.acescct.use.t: The default log2 color-grading space in ACES post-production.

space.acescg.desc.t: ACEScg — the Academy Color Encoding System's linear working space, defined by AMPAS in 2014 for CGI rendering and VFX compositing. On the wide AP1 primaries, it stores scene-referred light without a log curve, with headroom above white for highlights and light sources that would otherwise clip.

space.acescg.use.t: The standard in ACES-based VFX and animation pipelines.

space.acesproxy.desc.t: ACESproxy — the Academy's on-set monitoring and preview encoding, carrying ACES images on AP1 primaries as 10-bit, legal-range log code values over SDI. It is coarse and quantized, for on-set color decisions, dailies and viewfinder preview, not for storage, archiving or final grading: post works from the full ACES images.

space.acesproxy.loss-note.t: Integral SDI code values by design; decode-encode snaps to the 10-bit lattice.

space.acesproxy.use.t: On-set monitoring and dailies previews over SDI; not for final grading.

space.adx10.desc.t: ADX10 – Academy Density Exchange at 10 bits per channel (SMPTE ST 2065-3): a scanned color negative stored as Academy Printing Density, the density a print film's spectral sensitivities would see (ST 2065-2). Codes count up from the film base at 95, 500 per unit of red density as in Cineon; green and blue densities are scaled by 0.92 and 0.95 first. The Academy's input transform reaches ACES2065-1 through one fixed characteristic curve, a toe table then a straight line of gamma 0.55. The standard prefers ADX16; ADX10 serves 10-bit hardware and tops out at 1.856 of red density above the base.

space.adx10.use.t: Scanned film negatives entering ACES as 10-bit DPX, for archive, restoration and film-originated work.

space.adx16.desc.t: ADX16 – Academy Density Exchange at 16 bits per channel, the form SMPTE ST 2065-3 recommends: ADX10's printing-density metric in six more bits, four of precision and two of range: the film base at 1520 and 8000 codes per unit of red density (ADX16 = 16 × ADX10, exactly). Its codes reach 8 of red density above the base, room for the negative and internegative stocks that, the standard notes, exceed ADX10's 1.856. The Academy's input transform to ACES2065-1 is ADX10's after the code scaling.

space.adx16.use.t: Scanned film negatives entering ACES as 16-bit files, the standard's preferred form.

space.anlab.desc.t: ANLAB is the chromatic-valence opponent space Adams developed in 1942 and Nickerson extended in 1950, the direct ancestor of CIELAB. It runs each adapted tristimulus ratio through the Munsell Renotation System's empirical value function, then takes differences of the results to get lightness and two opponent channels. In 1976 CIELAB kept that logic but replaced the iterative Munsell function with a closed-form cube root.

space.anlab.successor-note.t: CIELAB kept its opponent logic and swapped the Munsell function for a cube root

space.anlab.use.t: Industrial color-difference measurement; superseded by CIELAB and CIEDE2000.

space.apple-rgb.desc.t: Apple RGB — the working space of classic Mac OS, modeled on Apple's original Trinitron CRT displays. It pairs a D65 white with a gamma of about 1.8, Apple's historic system default, and was a common Photoshop working space for years; legacy image files still carry it.

space.apple-rgb.successor-note.t: sRGB became the default of Windows, the web and Photoshop 5

space.apple-rgb.use.t: Mac and Photoshop working space (D65, γ 1.8) from the 13″ AppleColor monitor.

space.applelog.desc.t: Apple Log — Apple's log profile for ProRes Log recording, introduced with the iPhone 15 Pro in 2023 and integrated into Final Cut Pro's color tools. Its curve opens with a quadratic toe near black, then switches to log2 for the highlights, extending recordable dynamic range well beyond the phone's standard video profiles. It is defined over BT.2020 primaries; Apple Log 2 later kept the curve on a wider gamut.

space.applelog.use.t: Cinema-oriented log capture on iPhone Pro.

space.applelog2.desc.t: Apple Log 2 — Apple's second log encoding for iPhone video, specified in Apple's September 2025 white paper. It keeps the Apple Log transfer function unchanged, a log2 curve that rolls into a parabola near black to better hold negative noise values, so 18% grey still lands at 0.4883. What changes is the gamut: instead of the BT.2020 container Apple Log records into, Apple Log 2 encodes Apple Wide Gamut, a D65 primary set Apple optimized for its camera sensors in scene-referred work.

space.applelog2.use.t: Log capture on iPhone for grading and VFX; Apple's current log encoding (white paper, Sept 2025).

space.atd95.desc.t: ATD95 — Sherman Lee Guth's final ATD model (1995), a vision-science account of the opponent pathways. Retinal illuminance drives gain-controlled cone responses into two sequential opponent stages of A (achromatic), T (tritan, red-green) and D (deutan, yellow-blue) signals, modelling discrimination and adaptation data rather than appearance scales. Guth stressed it “cannot be considered a colour appearance model”; here it is the coordinate system of its second (large-field) stage, the one his hue and saturation predictions read from.

space.atd95.use.t: Historical vision-science model, kept for study.

space.awg3.desc.t: ARRI Wide Gamut 3 – the camera RGB primaries of ARRI's third color-science generation, published by ARRI in 2011 as ALEXA Wide Gamut RGB and renamed ARRI Wide Gamut 3 in the LogC4 specification. The primaries are virtual, placed to hold the colors the ALEXA sensor records rather than to match any display. This is the scene-linear form: decoded LogC3 data, scaled so a white diffusing reflector reads 1.0, with highlights above it. It is the gamut of the ALEXA Classic, XT, SXT, Mini, LF, Mini LF and 65 and the AMIRA.

space.awg3.successor-note.t: ARRI's fourth color-science generation arrived with the ALEXA 35

space.awg3.use.t: VFX and grading of ALEXA and AMIRA footage in LogC3; still active.

space.awg4.desc.t: ARRI Wide Gamut 4 – the RGB primaries of ARRI's fourth color-science generation, introduced with the ALEXA 35 in 2022 and paired with the LogC4 curve. Its red primary is ACES AP0's red and its green sits on AP0's red-green edge, so the gamut lies within AP0. This is the scene-linear form: decoded LogC4 data before any display transform, with highlights above 1.0.

space.awg4.use.t: Scene-linear gamut for VFX and grading of ALEXA 35 footage.

space.bestrgb.desc.t: Best RGB – Don Hutcheson's variant of Don RGB 4 with the red primary moved onto the spectral locus at 700 nm, to enclose the saturated reds and magentas of Fujichrome Velvia film, and a slightly more saturated green. Its blue, shared with Don RGB 4, lies just outside the locus, so about 3.5% of its code values encode no real color. Like Don RGB 4 it uses a D50 white and gamma 2.2 and is distributed as an ICC profile.

space.bestrgb.use.t: Editing saturated film scans; niche, distributed as an ICC profile.

space.betargb.desc.t: Beta RGB – a working space Bruce Lindbloom derived as the smallest RGB gamut that encloses a reference set of film, color-chart and printing colors, so it holds them with less wasted code range than larger spaces such as ProPhoto RGB. Its white is D50, the white of ICC profiles and Photoshop's Lab, chosen to avoid an adaptation step, and it uses gamma 2.2: Lindbloom's own perturbation analysis found an optimum near 2.12 and he kept the conventional value.

space.betargb.use.t: Capture, archiving and editing for high-end photo work; niche.

space.bmdfilm.desc.t: Blackmagic Film — Blackmagic Design's log curve for its Generation 5 color science, which debuted on the URSA Mini Pro 12K and rolled out across the Pocket Cinema Camera line. It combines a linear toe near black with a natural-log highlight region to hold detail across the sensor's full dynamic range for grading in DaVinci Resolve. It pairs with the BMD Wide Gamut Gen5 primaries and ships inside Blackmagic RAW (BRAW) footage.

space.bmdfilm.use.t: BRAW on Blackmagic's URSA Mini Pro and Pocket Cinema cameras with Gen 5 color science.

space.bmdwg.desc.t: Blackmagic Wide Gamut (Gen 5) – the camera RGB primaries of Blackmagic Design's Generation 5 color science, introduced in 2020 and paired with the Blackmagic Film Gen 5 log curve in Blackmagic RAW. All three of its primaries are virtual, outside the spectral locus, placed to hold what the sensor records. This is the scene-linear form, before the log curve, with highlights above 1.0.

space.bmdwg.use.t: Scene-linear gamut under Blackmagic Film Gen 5 for BRAW footage in VFX and grading.

space.brucergb.desc.t: Bruce RGB – a working space Bruce Fraser published in 1998 as a safe, output-oriented choice for Photoshop 5 users editing 8-bit images heavily. He designed it as a compromise between ColorMatch RGB, which clips printable cyans, and Adobe RGB (1998), which spends code values on colors few printers reach. It shares the red and blue primaries and D65 white of sRGB and Adobe RGB (1998), differs only in its green, and uses gamma 2.2.

space.cam02-lcd.desc.t: CAM02-LCD is a variant of the CAM02-UCS uniform color space that Luo, Cui & Li tuned in 2006 for large color differences, while most difference formulas target small ones. Like CAM02-UCS, it reprojects CIECAM02's lightness and colorfulness into a near-Euclidean Cartesian layout, with scaling calibrated against large-difference visual data.

space.cam02-lcd.successor-note.t: Rebuilt on CAM16 when CAM16 replaced CIECAM02

space.cam02-scd.desc.t: CAM02-SCD is a variant of the CAM02-UCS uniform color space that Luo, Cui & Li tuned in 2006 for small color differences. Like CAM02-UCS, it reprojects CIECAM02's lightness and colorfulness into a near-Euclidean Cartesian layout, with scaling calibrated against small, near-threshold visual differences.

space.cam02-scd.successor-note.t: Rebuilt on CAM16 when CAM16 replaced CIECAM02

space.cam02-scd.use.t: Small color-difference tolerance and QC judgments.

space.cam02-ucs.desc.t: CAM02-UCS is the uniform color space Luo, Cui & Li built on CIECAM02 in 2006. Its lightness and colorfulness pass through a compressive scale, so equal distances track equal perceived differences much more closely. In Cartesian coordinates it reads like CIELAB, only more perceptually uniform.

space.cam02-ucs.successor-note.t: Rebuilt on CAM16 when CAM16 replaced CIECAM02

space.cam02-ucs.use.t: ΔE computation and gamut mapping; still in wide use – matplotlib's viridis was designed in it.

space.cam16-lcd.desc.t: CAM16-LCD is a variant of the CAM16-UCS uniform color space that Li et al. tuned in 2017 for large color differences, the CAM16 counterpart to CAM02-LCD. It reuses compression coefficients from Luo, Cui & Li's 2006 work on uniform CIECAM spaces and, like CAM16-UCS, reprojects CAM16's lightness and colorfulness into a near-Euclidean Cartesian layout, with scaling calibrated against large-difference visual data rather than the small differences most formulas target.

space.cam16-lcd.use.t: Large color-difference and gamut-mapping comparisons; the default for that role.

space.cam16-scd.desc.t: CAM16-SCD is a variant of the CAM16-UCS uniform color space that Li et al. tuned in 2017 for small color differences, the CAM16 counterpart to CAM02-SCD. It reuses compression coefficients from Luo, Cui & Li's 2006 work on uniform CIECAM spaces and, like CAM16-UCS, reprojects CAM16's lightness and colorfulness into a near-Euclidean Cartesian layout, with scaling calibrated against small, near-threshold visual differences rather than the coarser ones CAM16-LCD targets.

space.cam16-scd.use.t: Small color-difference tolerance and QC comparisons; the default for that role.

space.cam16-ucs.desc.t: CAM16-UCS is the uniform color space Li et al. built on CAM16 in their 2017 paper. Its lightness and colorfulness pass through a compressive scale, so equal distances track equal perceived differences much more closely. In Cartesian coordinates it reads like CIELAB, only more perceptually uniform.

space.cam16-ucs.use.t: ΔE computation and gamut mapping; the default successor to CAM02-UCS.

space.cam16.desc.t: CAM16 is the color appearance model Li et al. introduced in 2017 as a simpler, more robust successor to CIECAM02. From the stimulus plus the surrounding light, the background and the eye's state of adaptation, it predicts how a color looks: lightness, colorfulness and hue, and in the full model also chroma, saturation and brightness.

space.cam16.use.t: Color-appearance modeling; the default replacement for CIECAM02 and the basis of Material Design's HCT.

space.cct-duv.desc.t: CCT + Duv — the lighting industry's two-coordinate description of near-white chromaticity. Correlated colour temperature locates the nearest point on the Planckian locus; Duv is the signed perpendicular distance from that locus in the CIE 1960 uv diagram (positive above the locus, conventionally greener; negative below it, conventionally pinker). Unlike CCT alone, the pair preserves both dimensions of chromaticity around the white-light region.

space.cct-duv.loss-note.t: Chromaticity only: luminance is discarded; the inverse reconstructs XYZ at Y=100.

space.cie-rgb.desc.t: CIE RGB — the color space built directly from the Wright and Guild color-matching experiments of 1928–1931, whose data became the foundation of CIE XYZ. Its primaries are single-wavelength lights, unlike the broadband primaries of any real display, with an equal-energy white. Nearly every later RGB space descends from it.

space.cie-rgb.successor-note.t: Its color-matching functions go negative, so the CIE adopted all-positive XYZ the same year

space.ciecam02.desc.t: CIECAM02 is the color appearance model the CIE published in 2002 to predict how a color looks to an observer under real viewing conditions, rather than only specify the stimulus. It passes cone responses through a chromatic-adaptation stage and an opponent-color stage, giving lightness, colorfulness and hue, plus chroma, saturation and brightness in the full model.

space.ciecam02.successor-note.t: CIECAM16 uses one matrix where it used two, and avoids its computational failures

space.ciecam16.desc.t: CIECAM16 is the color appearance model the CIE recommended in 2022 (CIE 248:2022) to replace CIECAM02 in color management. It is CAM16 with its post-adaptation compression continued as straight lines below and above a working range, which removes the infinite slope at zero and the ceiling at the top; inside that range it gives the same lightness, colorfulness and hue as CAM16 under the same viewing conditions.

space.ciecam16.use.t: Color management and cross-media reproduction; the CIE's recommended appearance model since 2022.

space.ciecam97s.desc.t: CIECAM97s is the interim color appearance model the CIE published in 1998 (CIE 131): one model for industry to share until a better one was formulated, and the direct predecessor of CIECAM02. A Bradford chromatic adaptation, with a nonlinear exponent on the short-wavelength channel, feeds Hunt–Pointer–Estévez cone responses and a hyperbolic compression, giving lightness, colorfulness and hue, plus chroma, saturation and brightness in the full model.

space.ciecam97s.successor-note.t: CIECAM02 made the chromatic adaptation linear and set lightness to zero at black

space.ciecam97s.use.t: Historical: the CIE's interim appearance model, superseded by CIECAM02.

space.cineon.desc.t: Cineon — Kodak's printing-density log encoding from the early 1990s, made for its Cineon film-scanning and digital-intermediate system. That system was the first to let film labs work on scanned negatives digitally instead of on an optical printer. Its 10-bit log curve maps negative density straight to code values, with reference black and white points chosen to mirror the film stock's response. It has no gamut of its own: scans inherit whatever primaries the film stock and scanner imply.

space.cineon.use.t: Digital intermediates; historical, surviving mainly through the DPX format it originated.

space.clog.desc.t: Canon Log — Canon's first cinema log gamma, introduced with the EOS C300 in 2011 to extend the dynamic range Cinema EOS cameras could capture ahead of grading. Its curve is symmetric around black, encoding a bit of below-black signal rather than clipping at zero. In this library it pairs with Canon's wide Cinema Gamut primaries, the same matrix shared with the later Canon Log 2 and Canon Log 3 curves.

space.clog.successor-note.t: Canon Log 2 held more of the newer sensors' dynamic range

space.clog.use.t: Cinema EOS camera log capture; largely superseded by Canon Log 2/3 but still supported for compatibility.

space.clog2.desc.t: Canon Log 2 — Canon's wider-latitude cinema log curve, introduced with the EOS C300 Mark II to capture more of the sensor's dynamic range than the original Canon Log. Its flatter, lower-contrast curve trades a coarser midtone step for extra stops of highlight and shadow information, intended for heavier grading later. It shares the Cinema Gamut primaries with Canon Log and Canon Log 3.

space.clog2.use.t: Cinema EOS log capture, alongside Canon Log 3.

space.clog3.desc.t: Canon Log 3 — Canon's balanced cinema log curve, added by firmware in 2016, a year after the EOS C300 Mark II shipped with Canon Log 2. It joins a log shadow region, a linear midtone and a log highlight region into one three-piece curve, aiming for close to Canon Log 2's dynamic range with gentler, easier-to-grade contrast. It shares the Cinema Gamut primaries with Canon Log and Canon Log 2.

space.clog3.use.t: Canon’s most widely used cinema log, a three-piece curve on Cinema Gamut.

space.cmy.desc.t: CMY is the subtractive color model of cyan, magenta and yellow alone, without CMYK's black channel. Each channel is the amount of ink absorbing its complementary part of white light, so all three at full strength approximate black.

space.cmy.successor-note.t: Impure inks mix to a muddy brown, so print added a black key ink

space.cmy.use.t: Three-ink subtractive counterpart to RGB and the arithmetic base of CMYK.

space.cmyk.desc.t: CMYK is the subtractive color model of offset and digital printing: cyan, magenta and yellow inks plus a separate black, K. Inks absorb light, the reverse of RGB displays emitting it, so in principle the three alone make black. Real inks are impure, so the black ink keeps dark tones neutral, saves ink and gives text and fine detail a cleaner edge.

space.cmyk.loss-note.t: The naive device equation: many CMYK values map to one RGB (max-K convention on the way back).

space.cmyk.use.t: Offset and digital printing; the prepress standard.

space.colormatch.desc.t: ColorMatch RGB – the RGB space of Radius's PressView calibrated monitors for professional graphic-arts work, shipped by Adobe as a Photoshop 5 working space. It uses P22-EBU phosphor primaries, a D50 white and gamma 1.8. Its gamut is close to sRGB's, slightly larger in the blue-greens and smaller in the red-blues, and it clips printable cyans that Adobe RGB (1998) keeps.

space.coloroid.desc.t: Coloroid — the Hungarian architectural color-order system, developed by Antal Nemcsics at the Budapest University of Technology and standardized as MSZ 7300. Grown from large-scale aesthetic experiments, it steps hue (A), saturation (T) and lightness (V) so they feel evenly spaced when composing whole environments.

space.coloroid.use.t: Architectural and urban color planning; standardized as MSZ 7300, still used in Hungary.

space.cubehelix.desc.t: Cubehelix is a hue, saturation, lightness model of RGB built on Dave Green's 2011 color scheme for astronomical images. Green's scheme spirals around the gray diagonal of the RGB cube from black to white, keeping its deviation from gray in a plane of constant NTSC luma so that brightness rises steadily. d3-color reads the spiral's parameters as coordinates: L is the luma 0.30R′ + 0.59G′ + 0.11B′, S scales the deviation from gray, H is its angle. Every RGB color has one (H, S, L) and converts back exactly, so it is a color space; a Cubehelix colormap is a path through it at fixed S from L = 0 to L = 1.

space.cubehelix.use.t: Colormaps and hue-rotating interpolation in d3 (interpolateCubehelix) and culori.

space.davinci.desc.t: DaVinci Wide Gamut — Blackmagic's wide gamut encoded with its DaVinci Intermediate log curve, the pair Blackmagic calls DaVinci Wide Gamut Intermediate, introduced in 2020 with DaVinci Resolve 17. Footage from any camera can be converted into it and graded consistently, as with ACES but native to Resolve. The curve encodes over 9 stops above mid-grey, keeping highlight and shadow detail for the creative grade.

space.davinci.use.t: The default log working space in DaVinci Resolve's color management.

space.dcdm.desc.t: DCDM — the Digital Cinema Distribution Master encoding inside every DCP (Digital Cinema Package) shipped to theatres, standardized by SMPTE under the DCI specification. It encodes CIE XYZ directly with a 2.6 power-law gamma rather than an RGB transfer curve, tying relative white to the DCI reference projector's calibrated luminance. It is display-referred and deliverable-only: mastering into DCDM is the last step before packaging.

space.dcdm.use.t: Theatrical DCP mastering, where it is mandatory (SMPTE ST 428-1).

space.dci-p3-plus.desc.t: DCI-P3+ – an expanded color gamut Canon added to the EOS C500 cinema camera's RAW development in a 2013 firmware update, wider than DCI-P3 but sharing its DCI white point (x 0.314, y 0.351). Its blue primary lies below the spectral locus (y −0.09), so part of its code range encodes no real color; Canon's Cinema Gamut, added in the same update, is wider still. Here it carries DCI-P3's pure gamma 2.6, as colour-science defines it, with the DCI white Bradford-adapted to D65 as in dci-p3.js.

space.dci-p3.desc.t: DCI-P3 — the digital cinema standard defined in SMPTE RP 431-2 for theatrical projection and mastering. It shares its wide primaries with Apple's Display P3 but pairs them with the DCI theatrical white point and a pure 2.6 gamma, while consumer display variants use D65 and an sRGB-like curve.

space.dci-p3.use.t: Digital cinema projection and mastering, the theatrical standard; the basis of Display P3.

space.dgamut.desc.t: D-Gamut – DJI's camera RGB primaries for its cinema color system, introduced in 2017 with the Zenmuse X7 and paired with the D-Log curve. DJI built it to cover Rec.709 and DCI-P3 with margin, and set each primary as nearly as possible on the line from D65 through the matching DCI-P3 primary, so hues hold when footage is gamut-mapped to P3. This is the scene-linear form, before D-Log, with highlights above 1.0.

space.dgamut.use.t: Scene-linear gamut under D-Log for VFX and grading of DJI Zenmuse and Ronin footage.

space.din99.desc.t: DIN99 is the uniform color space of the German standard DIN 6176:2001, written by the DIN colorimetry committee (FNF/FNL 2) so that plain Euclidean distance approximates the CIE94 color difference without CIE94's weighting functions. It takes D65 CIELAB, compresses lightness logarithmically, rotates the a*b* plane by 16°, shrinks the rotated yellow-blue axis to 0.7 and compresses chroma logarithmically; a99/b99 stay in the rotated frame. DIN 6176:2018 replaced it with the refitted DIN99o and moved this formula to an appendix.

space.din99.use.t: Industrial color-tolerance measurement (coatings, plastics); legacy, superseded by DIN99o in DIN 6176:2018.

space.din99c.desc.t: DIN99c is one of three refinements of the DIN99 uniform color space published in 2002 by Cui, Luo, Rigg, Roesler and Witt, fitted to combined small color-difference data so Euclidean distance performs close to CIEDE2000. Like its sibling DIN99d it corrects the blue region by mixing a share of Z into X before the CIELAB step; unlike DIN99d it keeps the CIELAB axis orientation (no rotation) and scales the b axis by 0.94 before the logarithmic chroma compression.

space.din99c.use.t: Euclidean color-difference research; not part of DIN 6176.

space.din99d.desc.t: DIN99d is a 2002 refinement of the DIN99 uniform color space by Cui, Luo, Rigg, Roesler and Witt, made to fix the original's uneven treatment of blue hues. It corrects the tristimulus values before the CIELAB step, then applies the family's usual hue rotation and logarithmic compression, so Euclidean distance tracks perceived difference more evenly around the hue circle than in DIN99 or CIELAB.

space.din99d.use.t: Industrial color tolerances (coatings, plastics, automotive); a niche alternative to CIEDE2000.

space.din99o-lab.desc.t: DIN99o Lab is a nonlinear remapping of CIELAB from the German color-difference standard DIN 6176. It is built so plain Euclidean distance approximates perceived color difference far more closely than in CIELAB: it compresses lightness and chroma logarithmically and rotates hue, correcting CIELAB's tendency to overstate differences between highly saturated colors.

space.din99o-lab.use.t: Coatings, plastics and automotive QC, standardized in DIN 6176; a lighter alternative to CIEDE2000.

space.din99o-lch.desc.t: DIN99o LCh is the cylindrical form of DIN99o Lab, the DIN 6176 color-difference space. As LCh does for CIELAB, it trades the rectangular axes for chroma and hue, a more direct handle on saturation and hue. Since DIN99o's Euclidean distance already approximates perceived difference, a plain chroma or lightness difference here is a meaningful tolerance metric, with no correction formulas.

space.din99o-lch.use.t: Adjusting chroma and hue tolerances in industrial QC.

space.dkl.desc.t: DKL — the cardinal-axis space of human color vision, proposed by Derrington, Krauskopf & Lennie in 1984 from recordings of neurons in the macaque lateral geniculate nucleus. Its three axes are the directions those neurons actually respond along: achromatic luminance, isoluminant red-green and tritan blue-yellow, all relative to an adapting white.

space.dkl.use.t: Vision-science stimulus design isolating cardinal color mechanisms; the field's standard framework.

space.dlog.desc.t: D-Log — DJI's log curve for its cinema-oriented cameras, including the Zenmuse X7 and Ronin 4D, made to keep dynamic range for grading rather than direct viewing. It pairs a linear toe near black with a log10 highlight curve, on the D-Gamut primaries built for those cameras' sensors.

space.dlog.use.t: DJI's cinema drone and gimbal cameras, the Zenmuse and Ronin lines.

space.donrgb4.desc.t: Don RGB 4 – a wide-gamut Photoshop working space from Don Hutcheson (HutchColor), with a D50 white and gamma 2.2, made to hold the color gamut of Ektachrome transparency film with virtually no clipping. It is distributed as an ICC profile. In Lindbloom's comparison it encloses 72.1% of the CIELAB gamut and all of the film and print color sets he tested except a sliver of the ColorChecker DC.

space.donrgb4.use.t: Editing transparency scans for photo and prepress; niche, distributed as an ICC profile.

space.dsh.desc.t: CIE DSH — dominant wavelength, saturation (excitation purity) and luminance, the classical Helmholtz coordinates for CIE 1931 chromaticity. In place of the x, y pair, a color is placed by the spectral wavelength it most resembles and how far it sits from white toward that spectral color, a way of naming hue and saturation that predates CIELAB-style opponent spaces. Non-spectral purples, which have no dominant wavelength, get a negative complementary wavelength.

space.dwg.desc.t: DaVinci Wide Gamut – Blackmagic Design's camera-agnostic RGB gamut, introduced in 2020 with DaVinci Resolve 17 together with the DaVinci Intermediate log curve. Blackmagic designed it to hold the vast majority of colors modern cameras capture, so footage from many sources can be stored and graded in one space before output to Rec.709 or Rec.2020. This is the scene-linear form, before the DaVinci Intermediate curve, with highlights above 1.0.

space.dwg.use.t: Scene-linear working gamut under DaVinci Intermediate.

space.ecirgb.desc.t: ECI RGB v2 – the RGB working space of the European Color Initiative for print-oriented image data, released in 2007 and standardized as eciRGB (2008) in ISO 22028-4. It keeps the NTSC 1953 primaries and D50 white of ECI RGB v1 (1999), but replaces v1's gamma 1.8 with the CIE L* curve: the code value is CIE lightness L* / 100, so equal code steps are equal lightness steps.

space.ecirgb.use.t: Print and prepress editing, standardized in ISO 22028-4:2023.

space.egamut.desc.t: E-Gamut – FilmLight's wide RGB gamut for its Baselight grading systems, paired with the T-Log curve as a camera-agnostic working space that footage from many cameras is converted into for grading. All three of its primaries lie outside the spectral locus. This is the scene-linear form, before T-Log, with highlights above 1.0.

space.ektaspace.desc.t: Ekta Space PS 5 – a working space photographer Joseph Holmes built for high-quality storage of transparency-film scans, sized to the film's gamut rather than to a display. Its blue primary lies outside the spectral locus, so a small part of its code range encodes no real color. It uses a D50 white and gamma 2.2 and is distributed as an ICC profile for Photoshop.

space.ektaspace.use.t: Editing transparency-film scans; niche, distributed as an ICC profile.

space.erimm.desc.t: ERIMM RGB — Kodak's Extended Reference Input Medium Metric RGB, a log-encoded, scene-referred format standardized in ISO 22028-3 as the extended-range member of the ROMM/RIMM family. It has ProPhoto RGB's wide primaries and D50 white, but its log curve holds scene exposures well beyond diffuse white, a much larger range than a linear or gamma-encoded format could hold.

space.erimm.use.t: Log archives of raw HDR scene data; niche and historical, one of Kodak's ROMM/RIMM family.

space.filmicpro.desc.t: Filmic Pro 6 Log — the log curve of Filmic Pro, a third-party iOS cinema camera app that gave iPhone footage a flat, grading-ready image years before Apple Log. Its curve mixes a square-root term and a natural-log term, set so full-scale input maps back to full-scale output. It has no published native gamut and is treated as a curve over linear RGB.

space.filmicpro.use.t: Log capture in the FiLMiC Pro iOS app, still available; overshadowed by native Apple Log since 2023.

space.flog.desc.t: F-Log — Fujifilm's log curve, introduced with the X-T2 in 2016 over HDMI only and recorded in-camera from the X-H1 in 2018. Firmware then brought internal F-Log to the X-T2 and other X-series and GFX cameras. A linear toe in the shadows and a logarithmic highlight rolloff extend recordable dynamic range for grading. It is defined over F-Gamut, whose primaries match ITU-R BT.2020.

space.flog.use.t: The standard log on Fujifilm bodies that lack F-Log2.
