space.flog2.desc.t: F-Log2 — Fujifilm's second-generation log curve, introduced on the X-H2S to capture roughly 14 stops of dynamic range, more than the original F-Log. Its curve is shallower than F-Log's, spreading those extra stops across the code-value range at the cost of needing more careful grading. It shares the F-Gamut primaries, matching ITU-R BT.2020, with F-Log.

space.flog2.use.t: Wider-dynamic-range log for Fujifilm X-series and GFX video, the flagship on newer bodies.

space.flog2c.desc.t: F-Log2 C — Fujifilm's F-Log2 curve recorded on F-Gamut C, a wider gamut than the BT.2020-matched F-Gamut that F-Log and F-Log2 use. Fujifilm's data sheet states the curve is identical to F-Log2, so 0%, 18% and 90% reflectance still land on 10-bit codes 95, 400 and 570; only the primaries change. F-Gamut C's red sits on ACES AP0 red, and its green and blue lie outside the spectral locus, so the gamut encloses BT.2020. Fujifilm added it to the X-H2, X-H2S and GFX100 II by firmware.

space.flog2c.use.t: The X-H2, X-H2S and GFX100 II, since a November 2024 firmware update.

space.gplog2.desc.t: GP-Log2 — GoPro's log profile for its MISSION 1 series cameras, documented by GoPro Labs in 2026. Like Protune it is a single pure-log curve, but with log base 600 instead of 113, packing up to 14 stops into a 10-bit signal over Rec.2020 primaries. The camera meters 18% grey to code 0.5416 (about 554 of 1023) and clips about 1.8 stops above diffuse white.

space.gplog2.use.t: Grading with GoPro Labs' GP-Log2 LUT generator.

space.gray.desc.t: Gray — a single relative-luminance channel, the Y of CIE XYZ, computed from linear-light RGB. Luminance (Y) measures physical light output; the luma (Y′) that video engineering computes from gamma-encoded RGB only approximates it.

space.gray.loss-note.t: Keeps luminance only; chromaticity is discarded.

space.gray.use.t: The basis of WCAG contrast ratios, derived from linear RGB.

space.hcg.desc.t: HCG — Hue, Chroma, Gray, a cylindrical RGB model that splits a color into its pure hue, the chroma (colorfulness) mixed into it and the gray added to dilute it. Unlike in HSL or HSV, chroma is an absolute measure of colorfulness, not relative to lightness or value, which suits additive mixing of hue and gray.

space.hcg.use.t: Colour-picker UIs; niche, mainly in JS colour libraries.

space.hcl.desc.t: HCL — a cylindrical Hue, Chroma, Luminance color space from the Chilliant rgb2hsv reference implementation. Hue and chroma work as in other cylindrical RGB models; luminance uses a gamma-weighted formula meant to track perceived brightness more closely than plain lightness or value. It is unrelated to CIE LCh, which is also sometimes called “HCL”.

space.hcl.use.t: Gamma-weighted-luminance picking in HLSL and shader code; niche, often confused with CIE LCh.

space.hct.desc.t: HCT — Google's color space for Material Design 3, introduced in 2021 for Android's Material You dynamic theming. It takes hue and chroma from CAM16, an appearance model that accounts for viewing conditions, and tone from CIELAB's L*, chosen because contrast and accessibility formulas already depend on it. From one seed color, a design system can then derive a full tonal palette with predictable contrast between any two tones.

space.hct.use.t: Tonal palettes for Android's Material You; the Material Design 3 standard.

space.hcy.desc.t: HCY — Hue, Chroma, Luma, a cylindrical color model devised by Kuzma Shapran and popularized by Chilliant for real-time shader use. Unlike HSI or HSL, its Y channel is the color's actual Rec. 601 luma rather than an average or extremum of the RGB channels, and chroma is scaled to the largest chroma the hue can reach at that luma. So Y tracks brightness better than HSL's lightness or HSV's value, though luma is not perceived lightness.

space.hcy.use.t: Real-time color grading in HLSL and GLSL shaders; niche.

space.hdr-cie-lab.desc.t: hdr-CIELAB — Fairchild & Wyble's 2010/2011 extension of CIELAB to high-dynamic-range imagery. CIELAB's cube-root lightness response was fit to ordinary display luminance and breaks down over HDR's wider range, so hdr-CIELAB swaps in a Michaelis–Menten response whose exponent adapts to scene luminance, echoing the eye's own adaptation.

space.hdr-cie-lab.successor-note.t: HDR image-difference work moved to HDR-native spaces such as ICtCp and Jzazbz

space.hdr-cie-lab.use.t: Image-difference work across wide luminance ranges; academic.

space.hdr-ipt.desc.t: hdr-IPT — Fairchild & Wyble's 2010/2011 extension of IPT to high-dynamic-range imagery. IPT's fixed power-law lightness response holds only over a narrow luminance range, so hdr-IPT replaces it with a Michaelis–Menten response whose exponent adapts to scene luminance, echoing the eye's own adaptation. IPT's hue linearity extends across HDR's much larger range.

space.hdr-ipt.use.t: Hue-linear appearance modeling; academic, not deployed in industry.

space.hellwig2022-hk.desc.t: The Helmholtz–Kohlrausch extension Hellwig, Stolitzka and Fairchild published in 2022 alongside the Hellwig 2022 model: of two colors with the same luminance, the more saturated one looks lighter. Fitted to earlier experimental data, it adds to the lightness J a term that grows with chroma and depends on hue; colorfulness M and hue h stay Hellwig 2022's.

space.hellwig2022-hk.use.t: Color-appearance modeling that predicts the extra lightness of saturated colors.

space.hellwig2022.desc.t: The Hellwig–Fairchild model, published in 2022, is a proposed refinement of CAM16, the model the CIE adopted as CIECAM16 (CIE 248:2022). It keeps CAM16's chromatic-adaptation transform, opponent-color dimensions and lightness correlate largely intact, and makes brightness a linear function of lightness, with revised chroma, colorfulness and saturation equations to match.

space.hellwig2022.use.t: Color-appearance modeling as a proposed refinement of CAM16; a simplified form drives the JMh space of ACES 2's output transform.

space.helmgen.desc.t: HelmGen is the generation space (GenSpace) of Helmlab, published by Görkem Yıldız in 2026 for UI design systems. It keeps Oklab's shape (cone-like LMS, a compressive transfer, an opponent matrix) but swaps the cube root for a depressed cubic y³ + αy = x, whose finite slope at zero removes the dark-end cusp singularities, then adds a mild chroma power, a piecewise lightness correction and a lightness-gated hue twist in the blues that keeps a blue-to-white gradient sky blue instead of lavender. Fit to gradient benchmarks rather than color-difference data; its sibling MetricSpace takes that role.

space.helmgen.use.t: Gradients, palettes and color-mix in design systems; shipped in Color.js 0.7.

space.helmgenlch.desc.t: HelmGen LCh is the cylindrical form of Helmlab's 2026 generation space: lightness, chroma and hue over HelmGen's opponent plane, the form for hue-led gradients, palette ramps and color-mix in design systems.

space.helmgenlch.use.t: Palettes and gradients in design systems; shipped in Color.js 0.7.

space.helmlab-metric.desc.t: Helmlab MetricSpace is the color-difference space of Helmlab, published by Görkem Yıldız in 2026 beside its generation sibling HelmGen. It starts as Oklab does (cone-like LMS, a power per cone, an opponent matrix), then adds hue-dependent corrections fit jointly to 3,813 judged color pairs (COMBVD): a Fourier hue rotation, a Helmholtz–Kohlrausch boost that lifts the lightness of vivid colors, lightness and chroma rescalings, a neutral correction that puts grays on a = b = 0, and a −28.2° turn of the a,b plane. White sits at L ≈ 1.12, and vivid colors reach higher still.

space.helmlab-metric.use.t: Color-difference research and Helmlab's ΔE; shipped in Color.js 0.7 without the neutral correction.

space.hpluv.desc.t: HPLuv is the pastel counterpart to HSLuv, from the same project by Alexei Boronine. Where HSLuv fits saturation to the sRGB gamut edge at each hue, HPLuv uses the largest circle that fits inside the gamut at each lightness, so every hue reaches the full saturation range. Lightness and hue come unchanged from LCHuv, as in HSLuv.

space.hpluv.use.t: Always-in-gamut pastel palettes; maintained alongside HSLuv.

space.hsi.desc.t: HSI — Hue, Saturation, Intensity, a cylindrical color model popular in image processing and computer vision. Intensity is the plain average of R, G and B, which separates brightness from color more cleanly than HSV or HSL for segmentation and feature extraction, at the cost of a more involved, arccos-based hue formula.

space.hsi.use.t: Image processing and computer vision; still used in segmentation and remote sensing.

space.hsl.desc.t: HSL — Hue, Saturation, Lightness, a cylindrical remapping of RGB first described by George Joblove and Donald Greenberg in 1978, beside Alvy Ray Smith's HSV. Hue is the angle around a color wheel, saturation is colorfulness relative to gray at that lightness, and lightness runs from black through the pure hue to white.

space.hsl.use.t: Color picking; standardized as CSS hsl().

space.hsluv.desc.t: HSLuv is Alexei Boronine's HSL built on CIELUV. In HSL, yellow and blue at S=100 are far from equally vivid; HSLuv rescales chroma per hue and lightness so S=100 always lands on the sRGB gamut edge, and the saturation slider behaves the same for every hue. Lightness and hue come unchanged from LCHuv.

space.hsluv.use.t: Even saturation across hues in design and palette tools; actively maintained, renamed from HUSL in 2018.

space.hsm.desc.t: HSM — Hue, Saturation, Mixture, proposed by Severino and Gonzaga (2009) for color image processing and tested on skin-color segmentation. Mixture is the weighted average (4R + 2G + B)/7, red weighted most after a 2:1 ratio of red to green cones, standing in for brightness; saturation is a color's distance from that gray relative to the farthest any color at the same mixture can reach, so it stays bounded at every mixture level.

space.hsp.desc.t: HSP — Hue, Saturation, Perceived brightness, a cylindrical color model built to fix HSL and HSV, whose lightness and value don't match how bright colors look. P weights R, G and B by the eye's sensitivity to each, so two colors with the same P look roughly equally bright, far closer than HSL or HSV get.

space.hsp.use.t: Hobbyist and creative-coding color pickers; niche.

space.hsv.desc.t: HSV — Hue, Saturation, Value, a cylindrical remapping of RGB from Alvy Ray Smith's 1978 paper. It shares HSL's hue angle but replaces lightness with value, the brightness of the strongest channel, so pure hues stay fully saturated across the whole brightness range instead of washing out toward white.

space.hsv.use.t: Color picking; the standard “wheel plus square” picker model.

space.hunt.desc.t: Hunt — Robert Hunt's colour appearance model (1982–1995), the most ambitious of the classical CAMs. It models cone and rod responses, luminance-level adaptation and surround induction, and predicts the full set of appearance correlates for related and unrelated colours. CIECAM97s and CIECAM02 are, in Fairchild's phrase, Hunt models simplified for practice.

space.hunt.use.t: Historical model kept for study; the direct ancestor of CIECAM97s and CIECAM02.

space.hunter-rdab.desc.t: Hunter Rd,a,b is Richard Hunter's earliest opponent-color scale, developed in 1943 for illuminant C so that early analog tristimulus colorimeters could report a color as reflectance plus red-green and yellow-blue values. Rd is the CIE Y value itself; a and b are linear differences of normalized X, Y, Z, scaled by a factor f(Y) that grows toward black to keep the dark end of the chromatic scales from collapsing. It preceded Hunter L,a,b (1958).

space.hunter-rdab.use.t: Single-number brightness/reflectance of neutral limestone-based powders; rarely used.

space.hwb.desc.t: HWB — Hue, Whiteness, Blackness, devised by Alvy Ray Smith in 1996 as an alternative to HSV for people mixing colors by hand. It describes a color as a pure hue diluted with some white and some black, the way painters tint and shade a pigment.

space.hwb.use.t: Tint and shade color picking; standardized as CSS Color 4's hwb().

space.iapbp.desc.t: IaPbP is a uniform color space for HDR and wide-gamut images published by Huang et al. in 2024. It keeps IPT's layout (cone matrix, per-cone nonlinearity, opponent matrix) but makes both matrices 4×4 projective transforms in homogeneous coordinates and replaces the power law with SA-PQ, a PQ-shaped curve fitted to a surround-aware contrast sensitivity function for a 500 lx room. The parameters were optimized jointly for uniformity, hue linearity and low crosstalk between lightness and chroma.

space.iapbp.use.t: Tone mapping and color difference in HDR/WCG imaging; research.

space.icacb.desc.t: ICaCb — an HDR opponent space designed by Fröhlich in 2017, built like ICtCp but re-optimized for just-noticeable-difference uniformity and straighter hue lines. XYZ passes through a dedicated cone matrix and the PQ (ST 2084) non-linearity before the opponent mix.

space.icacb.use.t: Research; re-optimized for JND uniformity versus ICtCp, not broadly adopted in industry.

space.ictcp-hlg.desc.t: ICtCp with the HLG transfer is the second ICtCp variant in ITU-R BT.2100: the same Rec. 2020 to LMS cone matrix as PQ ICtCp, but each cone signal is coded with the Hybrid Log-Gamma OETF on scene light, and the Ct and Cp rows are the PQ rows scaled by about 0.55 and 0.53.

space.ictcp-hlg.use.t: HLG HDR coding, standardized in BT.2100 beside the default NCL Y′C′bC′r.

space.ictcp.desc.t: ICtCp — Dolby's HDR opponent space, standardized in ITU-R BT.2100 for HDR television. Intensity rides the PQ curve, and the two chroma axes keep hue stable under big luminance changes.

space.ictcp.use.t: HDR grading and the ΔE-ITP difference metric; standardized in ITU-R BT.2100 for HDR production and programme exchange.

space.igpgtg.desc.t: IgPgTg is a color space Hellwig and Fairchild proposed in 2020 for hue linearity, where colors of one perceived hue share one hue angle. It follows IPT: a lightness signal from LMS cone responses plus two opponent channels, protan and tritan, named for the color-vision deficiencies their axes roughly align with. Where IPT was fit to visual hue data, IgPgTg was optimized so Gaussian-shaped spectra with one peak wavelength share one hue; it did well in the authors' hue-linearity experiment but poorly on existing visual data.

space.igpgtg.use.t: Hue-linearity research; academic, not widely deployed.

space.ihls.desc.t: IHLS, Improved HLS, is a 3D-polar remapping of RGB introduced by Allan Hanbury in 2003, building on a 2002 technical report with Jean Serra. Hue is the exact angle in the chromatic plane, saturation is max(R,G,B) − min(R,G,B) and brightness is Rec. 709 weighted luma. Saturation therefore stays small for every near-gray and does not depend on brightness, whereas HLS divides by lightness and can call a near-black color fully saturated.

space.ihls.use.t: Image analysis and color morphology; research niche.

space.ilog.desc.t: Insta360 I-Log — Insta360's log profile, here in the 10-bit container curve of its June 2026 white paper (revision 2026.05.20). A log10 curve rises from a short linear toe and holds scene reflectance from black to 2200%, about 7 stops over middle grey, on BT.2020 primaries with a D65 white. 0% lands at 0.0906 (10-bit code 93) and 18% grey at 0.4220 (code 432). The paper's version history shows the curve has changed: an initial version in 2024, a new transfer function for the 10-bit container in July 2025, and a bug fix before the final release.

space.ilog.use.t: Footage from Insta360's 10-bit I-Log cameras (X6, Luna Ultra), graded with Insta360's official I-Log LUTs.

space.ipt-ragoo.desc.t: Ragoo and Farup's 2021 re-optimization of IPT keeps Ebner and Fairchild's structure (XYZ to LMS matrix, signed power, opponent matrix) and refits its parameters: new cone primaries, exponent 0.4071 instead of 0.43, and a skew, tilt and rotation folded into the opponent matrix. The fit trades color order (hue linearity) against perceptual uniformity; the published setting improves STRESS by 14 % and the color-order metric by 37 % over IPT on the authors' own training data.

space.ipt.desc.t: IPT — an opponent color space built by Ebner & Fairchild in 1998 so lines of constant hue stay straight as saturation and lightness change, a property CIELAB lacks. A cone-response power law followed by an opponent matrix gives its lightness, red-green and yellow-blue axes.

space.ipt.use.t: Gamut mapping and image-difference metrics; still used, the structural ancestor of ICtCp.

space.iptpqc2.desc.t: IPT-PQ-C2 is Dolby's PQ-coded form of IPT, the signal of Dolby Vision profile 5, standardized as SMPTE ST 2128. Rec. 2100 linear RGB goes to LMS through a Hunt–Pointer–Estévez cone matrix with 2 % crosstalk, each cone is PQ-coded as in ICtCp, and Ebner and Fairchild's IPT matrix forms I, P and T. ST 2128 rules out mastering and production interchange.

space.iptpqc2.use.t: Consumer HDR streams in Dolby's proprietary ecosystem.

space.izazbz.desc.t: IzAzBz — the opponent-color stage inside Safdar et al.'s 2017 derivation of Jzazbz, before the final hyperbolic lightness compression that turns Iz into Jz. Iz is the achromatic response of the PQ-encoded LMS signal; az and bz carry the same red-green and yellow-blue chroma as Jzazbz.

space.izazbz.use.t: Intermediate opponent stage of the Jzazbz HDR derivation; research/internal use, foundation of the ZCAM appearance model.

space.jpeg.desc.t: JPEG YCbCr is the full-range YCbCr color space defined for JPEG still-image compression (ITU-T T.871 / JFIF), also called PC-range or full-swing YCbCr. Broadcast YCbCr reserves the ends of its 8-bit range as headroom and footroom for analog signal overshoot; JPEG YCbCr uses the full 0–255 range on all three channels, as computers store and display still images. Its coefficients are derived from BT.601, as in standard-definition video.

space.jpeg.use.t: JPEG/JFIF still images; formalized later as ITU-T T.871.

space.jzazbz.desc.t: JzAzBz — a perceptually uniform color space for high-dynamic-range imagery, published by Safdar et al. in 2017. It keeps small lightness and color differences uniform across HDR's much wider luminance and gamut range, where CIELAB's uniformity breaks down. Jz is a PQ-encoded lightness beside two opponent axes, az and bz; JzCzHz is its cylindrical form.

space.jzazbz.use.t: HDR color difference, in imaging research and color-management tools.

space.jzczhz.desc.t: JzCzHz — the cylindrical form of Safdar et al.'s 2017 JzAzBz, trading its az/bz opponent axes for polar chroma (Cz) and hue (Hz) while keeping its HDR perceptual uniformity.

space.jzczhz.use.t: HDR hue/chroma editing and gamut mapping; proposed in the CSS Color HDR module.

space.kelvin.desc.t: Kelvin — correlated color temperature (CCT), the scale that describes a light source's warmth or coolness by comparison with an ideal black-body radiator: about 2700 K for warm incandescent light, 6500 K and beyond for cool daylight. One temperature value maps to one point on the Planckian locus.

space.kelvin.loss-note.t: Any color projects to its nearest Planckian-locus CCT; only on-locus colors round-trip.

space.kelvin.use.t: White balance and CCT in photography, lighting and display calibration.

space.kim2009.desc.t: The Kim–Weyrich–Kautz model is a color appearance model published at SIGGRAPH 2009 from psychophysical data gathered at luminance levels up to 16,860 cd/m². It keeps CIECAM02's CAT02 adaptation but feeds absolute cone signals through a sigmoid set by the adapting luminance, then reads lightness through a media-dependent factor (LCD, transparency, CRT, paper).

space.kim2009.use.t: Cross-media reproduction and HDR tone mapping; academic.

space.kinelog3.desc.t: KineLOG3 — Kinefinity's log curve, introduced in September 2025, modelled on negative-film scanning: a log10 curve with a short linear segment below a small negative cut. It encodes Kinefinity Wide Gamut, the native gamut of the MAVO Edge 6K and MM2 LF, whose primaries all lie outside the spectral locus (green at y = 1.148, blue below zero). 18% grey lands at 0.3919, the spec's 39.2 IRE, and 90% reflectance at 0.5722.

space.kinelog3.use.t: Kinefinity cinema cameras on Kinefinity Wide Gamut; introduced September 2025.

space.lab-d65.desc.t: Lab-D65 is CIELAB, the CIE's 1976 perceptual space, anchored to D65, the white of sRGB, Rec. 709 and Display P3, instead of the D50 that ICC and CSS lab() use. Converting to and from those spaces then needs no chromatic-adaptation step. Otherwise it is CIELAB unchanged.

space.lab-d65.use.t: sRGB, Rec.709 and P3 work; common in display-color tooling.

space.lab.desc.t: CIELAB is the CIE's 1976 perceptual color space, the first widely adopted attempt to make Euclidean distance between coordinates track perceived color difference. Like the visual system beyond the retina, it splits color into lightness and two opponent axes. Color management conventionally anchors it to D50, the white of the ICC profile connection space and of CSS Color 4's lab(), not to any display's white point.

space.lab.use.t: Device-independent perceptual color specification; an ICC profile connection space and CSS Color 4's lab().

space.labh.desc.t: Hunter Lab is Richard Hunter's opponent-color scale for measuring surface color, published in its L, a, b form in 1958 and adapted to other illuminants through the Ka, Kb coefficients in 1967. It came years before CIELAB as one of the first practical attempts at a roughly uniform scale, built on square roots of the tristimulus values, which Hunter's photoelectric instruments could compute, where CIELAB uses cube roots. It is less uniform than CIELAB, but thanks to its head start, legacy industrial specifications still report in Hunter Lab units.

space.labh.use.t: Surface-color QC in paints, plastics, textiles and food; still specified in some industry standards.

space.lalphabeta.desc.t: lαβ is the color space Ruderman, Cronin and Chiao introduced in 1998 to decorrelate natural-scene color statistics, best known as the working space of Reinhard et al.'s 2001 color transfer. It converts RGB to LMS cone responses, takes their logarithm to compress dynamic range as the visual system does, then rotates them into three near-uncorrelated axes. Because natural images vary almost independently along these axes, matching one image's per-channel mean and spread to another's transfers the color mood of one photograph onto the other with minimal cross-channel artifacts.

space.lalphabeta.use.t: Color transfer between photographs; still used in image-processing research, popularized by Reinhard et al. (2001).

space.lch-d65.desc.t: LCh-D65 is the cylindrical form of Lab-D65, CIELAB reanchored to the D65 white of displays: its a and b axes become chroma and hue.

space.lch-d65.use.t: Saturation and hue handles in display-color tools, without chromatic adaptation.

space.lchab.desc.t: LCh(ab) is the cylindrical form of CIELAB, the CIE's 1976 perceptual space: its a/b axes become chroma and hue, so you adjust how saturated and which hue instead of red-green and yellow-blue offsets. Lightness carries over unchanged from Lab, and so does its uniformity.

space.lchab.use.t: Saturation and hue adjustment; underlies CSS Color 4's lch().

space.lchuv.desc.t: LCh(uv) is the cylindrical form of CIELUV, the CIE's 1976 companion to CIELAB: its u/v axes become chroma and hue, a handle for adjusting or comparing colors. Its hue angle comes straight from LUV's u′v′ diagram, where mixtures of lights fall on straight lines, so a light mixed with white keeps its hue angle. HSLuv and HPLuv rescale its chroma to fit the sRGB gamut.

space.lchuv.use.t: Saturation/hue adjustment in additive-mixture contexts; basis for HSLuv/HPLuv.

space.llab.desc.t: LLAB — Luo, Lo & Kuo's 1996 colour appearance model, developed as a candidate successor to CIELAB for cross-media image reproduction. It keeps CIELAB's opponent skeleton but swaps in a BFD chromatic-adaptation transform, a surround-dependent lightness exponent, and a logarithmic chroma compression that better tracks perceived colourfulness. CIECAM97s absorbed its ideas the following year, ending its short life as a standalone model.

space.llab.use.t: A historical candidate to succeed CIELAB, superseded by CIECAM97s and CIECAM02.

space.llog.desc.t: L-Log — Leica's log curve, first offered on the original SL (Typ 601) in 2015 and carried on to the SL2, SL2-S and later SL and Q3 cameras. A short linear toe in deep shadow gives way to a logarithmic response. It is recorded in a BT.2020 color container, the gamut Nikon's N-Log also uses; the original SL records BT.709.

space.llog.use.t: Leica SL-series video, native on the SL2-S, SL2 and SL.

space.lms.desc.t: LMS — the cone-response space of human vision, where L, M and S are the retina's long-, medium- and short-wavelength-sensitive cones. Describing color as the photoreceptors respond makes it the natural space for chromatic adaptation: predicting how a color must shift to look unchanged under another light. Competing cone and adaptation matrices model that differently, among them von Kries, Bradford, CAT02 and CAT16.

space.lms.use.t: Chromatic adaptation (von Kries, Bradford, CAT16); the basis of the CIECAM and CAM16 appearance models.

space.log3g10.desc.t: Log3G10 — RED Digital Cinema's current log curve, introduced in 2017 with the REDWideGamutRGB primaries as part of RED's IPP2 image pipeline. It encodes the sensor's wide dynamic range logarithmically, leaving grading latitude in both highlights and shadows.

space.log3g10.use.t: RED's default acquisition curve on Komodo, V-Raptor and Monstro/Helium cameras.

space.log3g12.desc.t: Log3G12 — an earlier RED Digital Cinema log curve, predating Log3G10 but on the same REDWideGamutRGB primaries. It allocates 12 stops of range above middle grey rather than Log3G10's 10, and its curve is sign-symmetric, encoding negative scene-linear values continuously instead of clipping them.

space.log3g12.successor-note.t: RED settled on Log3G10 as its one recommended curve

space.logc3.desc.t: LogC3 — ARRI's third-generation logarithmic encoding, used across the ALEXA camera line until LogC4 arrived with the ALEXA 35. Referenced to EI 800, it compresses the sensor's scene-linear exposure into a curve that keeps shadow detail and highlight headroom for grading, on the ALEXA Wide Gamut 3 primaries. For over a decade it was the dominant scene-referred camera space in digital cinema production.

space.logc3.successor-note.t: The ALEXA 35's wider dynamic range needed a new curve

space.logc3.use.t: Footage from the original ARRI ALEXA line; still widely supported in post.

space.logc4.desc.t: LogC4 — ARRI's fourth-generation logarithmic encoding, introduced with the ALEXA 35 in 2022. It compresses the sensor's 17 stops into a curve that keeps grading response uniform from deep shadow to specular highlight, on the ARRI Wide Gamut 4 primaries.

space.logluv.desc.t: LogLuv is Greg Ward Larson's high-dynamic-range pixel encoding, developed at Silicon Graphics and published in 1998 as the SGILOG codec of LibTIFF. It stores luminance as a base-2 logarithm and chromaticity as CIE 1976 u′v′, so 32 bits cover 38 orders of magnitude in 0.27% luminance steps and the whole visible gamut. Here it is the continuous conversion behind the 32-bit format: Le = 256·(log2 Y + 64), ue = 410·u′, ve = 410·v′, whose integer parts are the stored codes.

space.logluv.use.t: SGILOG compression in TIFF; legacy, still read and written by LibTIFF.

space.lrgb.desc.t: Linear-light sRGB — sRGB's D65 white point and primaries without its gamma-like transfer curve, so channel values are proportional to light intensity. Displays don't use it directly; color math does, since operating on gamma-encoded values gives wrong results.

space.lrgb.use.t: Color mixing and colorimetric conversion; foundational in color-managed rendering.

space.luv.desc.t: CIE L*u*v* (CIELUV) is the CIE's 1976 companion to CIELAB, another attempt at perceptual uniformity, built from a projected version of the CIE chromaticity diagram instead of Lab's opponent differencing. Its defining property is additivity: in its u′v′ chromaticity diagram (the CIE 1976 UCS), a mixture of two lights falls on the straight line between them, which Lab's a*b* plane cannot offer.

space.luv.use.t: Displays and stage lighting; still used, less common than CIELAB.

space.macboyn.desc.t: MacLeod–Boynton (MB) chromaticity — the cone-excitation diagram MacLeod & Boynton introduced in 1979, plotting color as relative long- and short-wavelength cone excitation on a constant-luminance plane. It isolates chromaticity at the cones themselves, not at the tristimulus values a display uses.

space.macboyn.use.t: Chromatic-discrimination research; the foundation of the DKL space.

space.maxwell.desc.t: Maxwell triangle — the barycentric chromaticity diagram for a trichromatic observer: three receptor catches, normalized to sum to one, plotted in an equilateral triangle with one receptor at each vertex. Human LMS catches, bee UV/blue/green catches and any other trichromatic phenotype share this geometry once their observer-specific catches exist. Here it is anchored to the library's human LMS cone space; other species' receptor models need external context and are out of scope.

space.maxwell.loss-note.t: Receptor magnitude is discarded; the inverse reconstructs LMS catches with sum=100.

space.maxwell.use.t: Comparative and biological vision; here in its human-LMS form.

space.milog.desc.t: Mi-Log — Xiaomi's log profile for the 14 Ultra and 15 Ultra smartphones, giving a flatter image with more grading latitude than the phones' standard color modes. Its curve has Apple Log's quadratic-toe-plus-log2 shape, tuned with Xiaomi's own constants, and is recorded in a BT.2020 color container.

space.milog.use.t: Log video on the Xiaomi 14 Ultra and 15 Ultra.

space.msh.desc.t: Msh is Kenneth Moreland's 2009 spherical form of CIELAB, introduced to design smooth diverging color maps for scientific visualization. M is the length of the (L*, a*, b*) vector, s the angle away from the L* axis (saturation) and h the hue angle in the a*b* plane. Interpolating linearly in Msh, with s driven to 0 at the midpoint, gives diverging maps whose lightness peaks smoothly at a near-white center; the cool-to-warm map built this way replaced the rainbow as ParaView's default in 2008 (release 3.4).

space.msh.use.t: Scientific visualization, as in ParaView and VTK's cool-to-warm map.

space.munsell.desc.t: The Munsell color system was devised by the American painter and art teacher Albert Munsell around 1905 to order colors by how they look, not by how pigments mix or lights combine. Its three axes are hue, value (lightness) and chroma, spaced so equal steps along any one look equal; a color is written “5R 5/10” for hue 5R, value 5, chroma 10. Visual experiments refined it into the 1943 Munsell Renotation, still its authoritative reference dataset.

space.munsell.loss-note.t: Renotation-table interpolation with an iterative inverse; exact only at table nodes.

space.munsell.use.t: Soil, geology and pigment/paint specification; still an active industry standard.

space.nayatani95.desc.t: Nayatani95 — Yoshinobu Nayatani's 1995 colour appearance model, the culmination of a line of research focused on illuminant-level effects: how the Hunt effect (colourfulness grows with luminance) and the Stevens effect (lightness contrast grows with luminance) reshape colour as adapting illuminance changes. Built on a von Kries cone stage with logarithmic opponent responses, it predicts brightness, lightness, chroma, colourfulness and saturation for related colours. Alongside Hunt's model it fed the CIE effort that became CIECAM97s.

space.nayatani95.use.t: Historical; folded into the CIECAM97s lineage.

space.nlog.desc.t: N-Log — Nikon's log curve, introduced with the Z6 and Z7 mirrorless cameras in 2018 and carried across the rest of the Z series. It pairs a cube-root shadow toe with a natural-log highlight region, unlike the log10 curves common elsewhere. Its gamut, N-Gamut, has the primaries of ITU-R BT.2020.

space.nlog.use.t: Video on Nikon Z-series mirrorless cameras.

space.ntsc.desc.t: NTSC RGB — the color primaries defined by the FCC in 1953 for the first US color television broadcasts, later formalized in ITU-R BT.470 System M. It is referenced to Illuminant C with a gamma of about 2.2; SMPTE-C and Rec. 709 later superseded its wide red and green primaries.

space.ntsc.successor-note.t: Receivers moved to brighter phosphors, and SMPTE-C standardized them

space.ohta.desc.t: The Ohta color space, introduced by Yu-Ichi Ohta, Takeo Kanade and Toshiyuki Sakai in 1980, decorrelates RGB into an intensity and two opponent chroma channels, chosen empirically to approximate the Karhunen–Loève transform (the statistically optimal decorrelation) of typical natural images. As an exact, invertible linear transform of RGB, it is cheap in both directions while still packing most of an image's variance into one channel. In segmentation of vegetation, fruit, flames and skin, that decorrelation makes thresholding more reliable than in RGB.

space.ohta.use.t: Computer-vision segmentation (vegetation, skin, flame); niche, still referenced in CV literature.

space.okhsl.desc.t: Okhsl is Björn Ottosson's 2021 hue-saturation-lightness remapping of Oklab for ordinary color pickers. Saturation is rescaled per hue and lightness so 100% always lands on the sRGB gamut edge, as in HSL; unlike HSL, built on gamma-encoded RGB, its lightness and hue track perception. Its siblings are Okhsv and Okhwb.

space.okhsv.desc.t: Okhsv is Björn Ottosson's 2021 hue-saturation-value counterpart to Okhsl, built on Oklab. Saturation and value are shaped so the space forms a cone that fits exactly inside the sRGB gamut. It keeps HSV's layout, with pure hues at full saturation and value, while lightness and chroma underneath are perceptually even.

space.okhwb.desc.t: Okhwb is the whiteness-blackness counterpart to Okhsv, extending Björn Ottosson's 2021 family of Oklab-based color pickers. As in HWB, a color is a pure hue mixed with some white and some black, the way painters mix tints and shades. Built on Okhsv, it inherits that space's perceptual evenness and stays within sRGB.

space.okhwb.use.t: Color picking; niche next to Okhsl and Okhsv.

space.oklab.desc.t: Oklab is Björn Ottosson's 2020 perceptual color space, a practical replacement for CIELAB in graphics and design work. It starts from how the eye's cone cells respond to light, then reshapes that signal so equal numeric steps look like equal changes in lightness, hue and chroma. Interpolating in it avoids the hue drift and desaturation that CIELAB and HSL produce.

space.oklab.use.t: Gradients and design tooling; underlies CSS Color 4's oklab() and oklch().

space.oklch.desc.t: OKLCH is the cylindrical form of Björn Ottosson's 2020 OKLab, designed so equal numeric steps look equal to the eye; it fixes CIELAB's blue shift.

space.oklch.use.t: Design-token palettes and CSS color authoring; the recommended CSS form.

space.oklrab.desc.t: OkLrab is Björn Ottosson's 2021 adjustment to Oklab's lightness channel: a toe curve compresses near-black values closer to how the eye perceives them. Plain Oklab's lightness diverges from CIELAB at the dark end, so blacks read lighter than they should; the toe corrects this and leaves the a and b axes untouched. It is used mainly for gamut mapping and lightness comparisons.

space.oklrab.use.t: Dark-tone gamut mapping; niche, in technical tools.

space.oklrch.desc.t: OkLrch is the cylindrical form of OkLrab, Björn Ottosson's toe-mapped variant of Oklab: its a/b axes become chroma and hue, and the corrected darks carry over.

space.oklrch.use.t: Palettes and gamut mapping that need accurate darks; niche.

space.olog.desc.t: O-Log — OPPO's log profile for its Find X8 Ultra-era smartphones. Apple Log and Xiaomi's Mi-Log are two-piece curves; O-Log is one pure natural-log function across the whole tonal range, with no separate toe near black. It is recorded in a BT.2020 color container.

space.olog.use.t: Log video on OPPO Find X8 Ultra-era phones.

space.olog2.desc.t: O-Log2 – OPPO's second smartphone log profile, released in 2026. OPPO publishes LUTs and an ACES transform for it but, as of October 2026, no white paper. Like O-Log it is a single pure-log curve with no toe segment, now in base 2 rather than e: scene-linear 0 encodes to 0.1199, 18% grey to 0.4879 and diffuse white to 0.6942. It is recorded in a BT.2020 color container with a D65 white.

space.orgb.desc.t: oRGB is an opponent color space for computer graphics, published by Margarita Bratkova, Solomon Boulos and Peter Shirley in 2009. A fixed matrix turns gamma-encoded R′G′B′ into luma plus two chroma axes, then a piecewise rotation of the hue angle puts yellow opposite blue and red opposite green, following Hering's opponent model. It keeps HSV-like simplicity while giving axes suited to color adjustment, cool-to-warm shading and color transfer.

space.osaucs-ee.desc.t: Log-compressed OSA-UCS is the space in which plain Euclidean distance is ΔE_E, the color-difference formula for small to medium differences that Claudio Oleari (Parma), Manuel Melgosa and Rafael Huertas (Granada) published in 2009. It takes OSA-UCS lightness and Oleari's opponent coordinates G, J (logarithms of tristimulus ratios, scaled by lightness), compresses lightness and chroma logarithmically and keeps hue. Its authors found ΔE_E statistically equivalent to CIEDE2000 on many available visual datasets.

space.osaucs-ee.use.t: Research on small to medium color differences and image-difference metrics (S-DEE, WLF-DEE); far less used than CIEDE2000.

space.osaucs.desc.t: OSA-UCS (Uniform Color Scale) is a color space developed by an Optical Society of America committee and published in 1974, closely associated with David MacAdam's work on the project. It aims for equal numerical distances to match equal perceived differences in every direction, for clearly visible steps rather than near-matches. The committee sampled it on a cubic close-packed lattice, so each sample color sits one equal step from 12 neighbors.

space.osaucs.use.t: Large-step color-difference work in industry and science; legacy, niche next to CIELAB and CIELUV.

space.ostwald.desc.t: Ostwald — Wilhelm Ostwald's colour system (Die Farbenlehre, 1917–1923), ordering colour as mixtures of exactly three sensations: white, black and a “full colour” (Vollfarbe). His full colours are ideal semichromes: optimal colours that reflect 100% over the half-spectrum bounded by a complementary wavelength pair and 0% elsewhere, the most saturated object colours physically possible for their hue. Every colour is then w·White + b·Black + f·FullColour with w+b+f=1, arranged as a double cone. The physical atlas died with its licensing; the ideal system is pure mathematics over the CIE observer, and that is what ships here.

space.ostwald.use.t: Historical double-cone colour-order system, kept for study.

space.p3-linear.desc.t: Linear-light Display P3 — the gamma-free form of Apple's Display P3: the same DCI-P3-derived primaries and D65 white point, with channel values proportional to light intensity.

space.p3-linear.use.t: Color math on Display P3 values, before re-encoding.

space.p3.desc.t: Display P3 — Apple's wide-gamut display space, introduced with the 2015 iMac and standardized into CSS Color 4 as `display-p3`. It keeps sRGB's transfer curve and D65 white but adopts the wider DCI-P3 film primaries, covering about 25% more colors.

space.p3.use.t: Apple devices, the default on iPhone, iPad and Mac; standardized in CSS Color 4.

space.pal.desc.t: PAL/SECAM RGB — the primaries of 625-line analogue television across Europe and much of the world, defined in EBU Tech 3213 and ITU-R BT.470 (System B/G). It has sRGB's D65 white but a slightly different green primary, so it is a separate gamut from Rec. 709 and the one for archival PAL or SECAM material. BT.470 assumes a display gamma of 2.8 for it, against 2.2 for NTSC.

space.panalog.desc.t: Panalog — the log curve of the Panavision Genesis, a digital cinema camera developed with Sony and released in 2005. Modeled on Kodak's Cineon printing-density curve with its own black and white points, it let Genesis footage drop into Cineon-based post pipelines, as RED's REDLogFilm later did for RED footage. Panavision never published a gamut for it, so here it is a curve over linear RGB.

space.panalog.retired.t: Recorded only by the Panavision Genesis

space.photoycc.desc.t: PhotoYCC is the color encoding Kodak developed in 1992 for Photo CD, to carry scanned film into a digital, display-oriented format. Film holds a wider gamut and dynamic range than CRT monitors of the time could show, so PhotoYCC extends the Rec. 709 curve into an odd-symmetric function that keeps scene-referred colors and highlights beyond the [0,1] display range, stored as 8-bit luma (Yc) and two chroma channels (C1, C2). Photofinishing labs could scan a roll once and make prints, monitor previews and digital copies from one master.

space.photoycc.use.t: Photo CD scans; obsolete since Photo CD was discontinued.

space.poirson-wandell.desc.t: Poirson–Wandell opponent space is the pattern-color-separable space of Allen Poirson and Brian Wandell (1993): one luminance and two chromatic channels, linear in cone or XYZ coordinates, fitted so that the perceived color of a pattern and its spatial form separate. S-CIELAB (Zhang and Wandell, 1996) blurs an image in it with one spatial kernel per channel before converting to CIELAB. The channels are not normalized to a white: D65 has small chromatic values.

space.poirson-wandell.use.t: S-CIELAB and other spatial color-difference metrics: filter here, then go to CIELAB.

space.prismatic.desc.t: Prismatic is a four-channel remapping of RGB by Peter Shirley and David Hart, written up in 2015 after they used it for color edits in the iPhone photo app Subjective. Hue is the Maxwell color triangle in barycentric form, (ρ, γ, β) = (R, G, B) / (R + G + B), and lightness is HSV's V = max(R, G, B), so every cross-section is the same triangle and the whole volume is a prism. Because a mix of two RGB colors lands on the straight line between their hues, hue mixing, saturation edits (s = 1 − 3·min(ρ, γ, β)) and palette clamping stay simple arithmetic.

space.prismatic.use.t: Palette reduction in photo apps; niche.

space.prolab.desc.t: proLab is a projective perceptual color space proposed by Konovalenko and colleagues in 2021. Where CIELAB applies a separate cube root to each XYZ channel, proLab applies one projective transform, so straight lines of additive light mixing stay straight, while distances still track human discrimination thresholds as CIELAB's do.

space.prolab.use.t: Image processing that must preserve linear mixtures; niche.

space.prophoto-linear.desc.t: Linear-light ProPhoto RGB — Kodak's ProPhoto (ROMM) RGB without its transfer curve: the same very wide primaries and D50 white, with channel values proportional to light. Color math on ProPhoto images happens here, before ProPhoto's curve is reapplied.

space.prophoto-linear.use.t: Raw-photo color math on ProPhoto (ROMM) RGB values.

space.prophoto.desc.t: ProPhoto RGB — Kodak's working space for high-end digital photography, also known as ROMM RGB. Its primaries reach beyond human vision, giving it one of the largest gamuts of any standard RGB space, with a D50 white point.

space.prophoto.use.t: High-end digital photography and raw processing; a common working space.

space.protune.desc.t: Protune — GoPro's flat color profile for its Hero action cameras, with minimal in-camera sharpening, saturation and contrast so footage keeps more room for color correction. One natural-log curve covers the whole tonal range, simpler than cinema cameras' multi-segment curves, over the Protune Native primaries.

space.protune.use.t: GoPro Hero action cameras; still on modern Hero output.

space.ral-design.desc.t: RAL Design System+ is RAL gGmbH's system of about 1,825 colors, each defined by a CIELAB hue angle, lightness and chroma. The older RAL Classic colors exist only as physical swatches; every RAL Design code is a point you can compute, with no chip to match by eye.

space.ral-design.use.t: European paint, coatings and architectural color specification; an active standard.

space.rec2020-display.desc.t: Rec. 2020 display is Rec. 2020 as a reference monitor shows it: BT.2020 primaries and D65 white, decoded by the ITU-R BT.1886 reference EOTF with zero black level and unit gain, a pure 2.4 power over the extended range. CSS Color 4 defines color(rec2020 …) this way. rec2020 keeps the BT.2020 camera curve, so the same three numbers name different colors in the two spaces.

space.rec2020-display.use.t: CSS color(rec2020 …); display-referred UHD video on a BT.1886 monitor.

space.rec2020-linear.desc.t: Linear-light Rec. 2020 — the UHDTV standard ITU-R BT.2020 without its transfer curve: the same very wide primaries and D65 white, with channel values proportional to light. Color math is accurate here; the Rec. 2020 curve is reapplied for delivery.

space.rec2020-linear.use.t: A UHD and HDR grading working space.

space.rec2020.desc.t: Rec. 2020 — the ITU-R BT.2020 standard for the gamut and transfer function of ultra-high-definition television. Its curve keeps Rec. 709's piecewise shape; its far wider gamut, close to the limits of human vision, is the target for 4K and 8K broadcast and streaming.

space.rec2020.use.t: The standard gamut for 4K/8K UHDTV broadcast and HDR.

space.rec2100-hlg.desc.t: Rec. 2100 HLG — Hybrid Log-Gamma, the HDR transfer function the BBC and NHK developed for broadcast, one of the two in ITU-R BT.2100. Where PQ encodes absolute luminance, HLG stays scene-referred: ordinary gamma near black, a log curve for highlights, so an unmodified SDR display still shows a reasonable picture without metadata.

space.rec2100-hlg.use.t: The standard HDR transfer function for live broadcast, scene-referred.

space.rec2100-linear.desc.t: Rec. 2100 Linear — the linear-light RGB of ITU-R BT.2100 before either HDR curve is applied: display light under PQ, scene light under HLG. It has Rec. 2020's wide primaries and white point, with headroom above reference white for specular highlights.

space.rec2100-linear.use.t: Linear-light HDR grading and gamut mapping, beneath Rec. 2100's PQ (display light) and HLG (scene light).

space.rec2100-pq.desc.t: Rec. 2100 PQ — ITU-R BT.2100's HDR RGB encoding: Rec. 2020 primaries with the Perceptual Quantizer transfer function (SMPTE ST 2084), developed by Dolby. Unlike SDR gamma, PQ encodes absolute display luminance, so a code value means the same luminance on any display, whatever its peak.

space.rec2100-pq.use.t: HDR10 and most HDR streaming and mastering.

space.rec709-display.desc.t: Rec. 709 display is Rec. 709 as a studio reference monitor shows it: BT.709 primaries and D65 white, decoded by the ITU-R BT.1886 reference EOTF with zero black level and unit gain, which leaves a pure 2.4 power. rec709 carries the camera curve instead; BT.709 itself names BT.1886 as the reference monitor's decoding, and the two curves are not inverses, so the same code values name different light in the two spaces.

space.rec709-display.use.t: Display-referred HD video: what a BT.1886 monitor emits for Rec. 709 code values.

space.rec709.desc.t: Rec. 709 — the ITU-R BT.709 standard for HDTV primaries and transfer function. It has the same primaries and D65 white as sRGB; only the curve differs, a camera OETF made for broadcast cameras instead of computer displays.

space.redlog.desc.t: REDLog — RED Digital Cinema's original log curve, from the RED ONE, the company's first digital cinema camera, released in 2007. It pairs with REDcolor, RED's earliest gamut, and was RED's default log until REDLogFilm, and later the Log3G10/REDWideGamutRGB pair of current RED cameras, replaced it.

space.redlog.successor-note.t: REDLogFilm matched Cineon, so RED footage fit film pipelines

space.redlog.use.t: RED ONE digital cinema footage, before REDLogFilm and Log3G10.

space.redlogfilm.desc.t: REDLogFilm — RED Digital Cinema's second log curve, matching Kodak's Cineon printing-density curve exactly so RED footage fit Cineon-based film pipelines. It keeps REDLog's REDcolor primaries and came between REDLog and the Log3G10/REDWideGamutRGB pair of current RED cameras.

space.redlogfilm.successor-note.t: RED's IPP2 pipeline replaced it with Log3G10

space.redlogfilm.use.t: RED footage in film-style pipelines, before Log3G10 and REDWideGamutRGB.

space.rg.desc.t: rg chromaticity — the RGB analog of CIE xy: R, G and B divided by their sum, so overall intensity drops out and only the color proportions remain. With brightness gone, it describes a surface's color more robustly to lighting changes than raw RGB.

space.rg.loss-note.t: Chromaticity only: overall intensity is discarded.

space.rgb-display.desc.t: sRGB 2.2 display is sRGB as the standard's reference display decodes it: sRGB primaries and D65 white with a pure 2.2 power and no linear toe. IEC 61966-2-1 characterizes its reference display by that exponent and writes the piecewise curve, toe included, as the encoding. Decoding with 2.2 renders shadows darker than the piecewise inverse does: signal 0.1 gives 0.63 % of white instead of 1.00 %.

space.rgb-display.use.t: What a display calibrated to a 2.2 power shows for sRGB-encoded values.

space.rgb.desc.t: sRGB — the standard RGB color space HP and Microsoft created in 1996, later standardized as IEC 61966-2-1. It has a D65 white point and a piecewise, gamma-like curve tuned to typical displays.

space.rgb.use.t: The web and untagged images; the dominant consumer-display standard.

space.rimm.desc.t: RIMM RGB — the scene-referred counterpart to Kodak's ProPhoto (ROMM) RGB, standardized in ISO 22028-3. It keeps ProPhoto's very wide primaries and D50 white with a camera-style curve that has headroom above diffuse white, so scene exposures that would otherwise clip survive the pipeline until output-referred rendering.

space.rlab.desc.t: RLAB is the color appearance model Mark Fairchild published in 1996 to predict how colors reproduce across media and viewing conditions, such as matching a print to how the image looked on a display. It adapts cone responses to a reference viewing condition with a von Kries-style transform through Hunt–Pointer–Estévez fundamentals, then maps them into a CIELAB-like lightness and opponent space, keeping CIELAB's structure while accounting for the surround and adaptation effects plain CIELAB ignores. It was among the first appearance models built for cross-media reproduction.

space.rlab.use.t: Matching print and display reproductions; academic, superseded by CIECAM02 and CAM16.

space.russellrgb.desc.t: Russell RGB – a working space photographer Russell Cottrell derived in 2011 by extending Bruce Lindbloom's Beta RGB into the cyans and blues, because the gamuts of his 10- and 12-ink pigment inkjet printers slightly exceeded Beta RGB there. It uses Cottrell's preferred 5500 K (D55) reference white and gamma 2.2, and is distributed as an ICC profile made in Photoshop.

space.rwg.desc.t: REDWideGamutRGB – RED Digital Cinema's standardized camera RGB, introduced in 2017 with the IPP2 image pipeline and paired with the Log3G10 curve. RED designed it to encompass every color a RED camera can generate without clipping, which puts its green primary far outside the spectral locus (y ≈ 1.49). This is the scene-linear form, before Log3G10, with highlights above 1.0.

space.rwg.use.t: Scene-linear gamut under Log3G10 and Log3G12 for VFX and grading on RED's IPP2 cameras.

space.ryb.desc.t: RYB is the traditional artists' color wheel with red, yellow and blue as primaries, taught in painting and design long before RGB or CMYK existed. It models how pigments mix on a palette: blue and yellow paint make green, while blue and yellow light add to grey. This version follows Johannes Itten's chromatic wheel from his Bauhaus color theory, still a standard reference for teaching color harmony.

space.ryb.use.t: The common teaching wheel in art and design, after Itten's Bauhaus color theory.

space.samsunglog.desc.t: Samsung Log — Samsung's log profile for Galaxy phones, introduced with the Galaxy S25 series in January 2025 and specified in Samsung's 2025 white paper. Two log10 segments meet at 1% reflectance: below it a mirrored segment bends the toe into an S-shape that keeps more shadow gradation, above it the main segment carries the highlights to the white limit at scene 12.0, about 6 stops over middle grey. The signal sits in a BT.2020 container with a D65 white; 18% grey lands at 0.5279, 10-bit code 540.

space.samsunglog.use.t: Galaxy S25 series and S24 series via One UI 7, graded with Samsung's Rec.709 LUT.

space.scam.desc.t: sCAM is the simple color appearance model Li and Luo published in 2024 together with its uniform space sUCS. It takes D65-referred XYZ, adapts it to the viewing conditions (adapting luminance, background, surround) and reads lightness, colorfulness and hue off sUCS, with brightness, vividness, blackness, whiteness and depth as further correlates. Its pipeline is shorter than CAM16's and inverts in closed form; this is its J, M, h form.

space.scrgb.desc.t: scRGB — a linear-light extension of sRGB, standardized as IEC 61966-2-2, that carries wide-gamut and HDR signals through an ordinary sRGB pipeline. It keeps sRGB's primaries and D65 white, drops the gamma curve and allows values far outside 0–1, for colors brighter or more saturated than sRGB can show.

space.scrgb.use.t: Linear-light HDR; Windows composes its HDR desktop in FP16 scRGB.

space.sgamut3-venice.desc.t: Venice S-Gamut3 – S-Gamut3 as Sony's Venice cinema camera records it, under S-Log3. In 2020 Sony gave the Academy a separate Venice input transform, whose matrix to ACES differs from the generic S-Gamut3 one (slog3) by up to 0.054 per coefficient. Sony prints only that matrix; the primaries here are derived from it at a D65 white. Their triangle covers 8% more xy area than generic S-Gamut3's without enclosing it.

space.sgamut3-venice.use.t: Footage from Sony's Venice camera recorded in S-Log3/S-Gamut3, through its own ACES input transform.

space.sgamut3.desc.t: S-Gamut3 – Sony's wide camera RGB, introduced in 2014 alongside the S-Log3 curve. It carries the same primaries as the original S-Gamut that S-Log and S-Log2 recorded, so one matrix serves all three Sony logs here; the narrower S-Gamut3.Cine variant is a separate space (sgamut3cine). This is the scene-linear form, before the log curve, with highlights above 1.0.

space.sgamut3.use.t: Scene-linear gamut for VFX and grading of Sony footage; as S-Gamut, also under S-Log and S-Log2.

space.sgamut3cine-venice.desc.t: Venice S-Gamut3.Cine – S-Gamut3.Cine as Sony's Venice cinema camera records it, under S-Log3. Its 2020 Academy input transform, a pair with Venice S-Gamut3's, carries a matrix to ACES that differs from the generic S-Gamut3.Cine one (sgamut3cine) by up to 0.052 per coefficient. Sony prints only that matrix; the primaries here are derived from it at a D65 white. Their triangle covers 7% more xy area than generic S-Gamut3.Cine's without enclosing it.

space.sgamut3cine-venice.use.t: Footage from Sony's Venice camera recorded in S-Log3/S-Gamut3.Cine, through its own ACES input transform.

space.sgamut3cine.desc.t: S-Gamut3.Cine — Sony's cinema variant of S-Gamut3, carried here with the S-Log3 curve it is recorded with (menu name “S-Gamut3.Cine/S-Log3”). Sony designed it to resemble a negative-film scan and to sit slightly wider than DCI-P3, so footage grades to DCI-P3 or Rec. 709 with less correction than full S-Gamut3 needs. That made it the common pick on Alpha and FX-line cameras when a production skips a heavy grade; full S-Gamut3 (see slog3) stays the wide-archive choice.

space.sgamut3cine.use.t: Sony's common cine setting for grades bound for P3 or 709, recorded with S-Log3.

space.slog.desc.t: S-Log — Sony's first log curve, introduced on the F35 and F3 cameras to capture more dynamic range than ordinary video gammas allowed. Paired with the S-Gamut primaries, it was made for scene-referred capture ahead of grading; S-Log2 and then S-Log3 soon refined its tonal placement.

space.slog.successor-note.t: S-Log2 rescaled it to hold more of the sensor's range

space.slog.use.t: F35 and F3 footage; kept for archival compatibility.

space.slog2.desc.t: S-Log2 — Sony's second log curve, a rescaled S-Log that captures more of the camera's dynamic range and improves shadows. It shares the S-Gamut primaries with S-Log and S-Log3. Sony offers it beside S-Log3, not replaced by it, on many cameras, for finer gradation in the mid-to-high tones.

space.slog2.use.t: Sony's second-generation cinema log (F65, F55 and F5 era).

space.slog3.desc.t: S-Log3 — Sony's current log curve, modeled on the tonal placement of film-scan logs like Cineon, so it grades more intuitively than the earlier S-Log curves. It pairs with S-Gamut3; the narrower S-Gamut3.Cine variant, closer to DCI-P3 for productions that skip a full grade, is a separate color space.

space.slog3.use.t: Sony CineAlta, Venice and Alpha cameras with S-Gamut3; the recommended acquisition setting.

space.smpte-240m.desc.t: SMPTE 240M — the interim analog HDTV standard SMPTE published in 1988, before Rec. 709 was finalized. It shares SMPTE-C's broadcast primaries and D65 white but has its own transfer function, a gamma-like curve with a linear segment near black, distinct from the BT.601 and BT.709 curves.

space.smpte-240m.successor-note.t: Rec. 709 became the worldwide HDTV standard

space.smpte-c.desc.t: SMPTE-C is the RGB primary set the Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers standardized (SMPTE 170M) for 525-line NTSC broadcast in North America. It replaced the 1953 FCC/NTSC primaries with phosphors that picture tubes of the time could actually produce, with a D65 white. As an RGB space it shares its transfer curve with Rec. 709 and BT.601 video.

space.smpte-c.use.t: NTSC broadcast in North America (RP 145); a historical analog reference.

space.srlab2.desc.t: SRLAB2 is Jan Behrens' combination of CIELAB and CIECAM02. It adapts color with CIECAM02's CAT02 instead of CIELAB's simpler, less accurate step, then applies a CIELAB-style cube-root opponent stage. It is more perceptually uniform than CIELAB, especially for saturated colors, yet as easy to compute and invert as Lab, without CIECAM02's viewing-condition machinery.

space.srlab2.use.t: CIELAB/CIECAM02 hybrid for more perceptually-uniform color-difference work; niche open alternative to Lab.

space.sucs.desc.t: sUCS is the simple uniform color space Li and Luo published in 2024 as the base of their simple color appearance model, sCAM. It aims for the uniformity of CAM16-UCS, where equal distances mean equal perceived differences, through a far lighter pipeline than CAM16, and needs no viewing-condition parameters.

space.sucs.use.t: Color difference, as a lighter alternative to CAM16-UCS and Oklab.

space.tlog.desc.t: T-Log — FilmLight's log curve for its Baselight grading systems, paired with the wide E-Gamut primaries. It is a near-pure log with a linear extension below zero, so noise and sub-black signal pass without the harsh clipping a pure log would give. Baselight facilities use T-Log/E-Gamut the way others use ACES or DaVinci Wide Gamut: a common space for footage from many cameras.

space.tlog.use.t: Grading in Baselight, on a Cineon-derived curve.

space.tsl.desc.t: TSL (Tint, Saturation, Lightness) is a cylindrical re-encoding of RGB that Terrillon and Akamatsu introduced in 2000 to detect human skin in images. Separating chromaticity (tint, saturation) from lightness packs skin pixels into a tighter, more separable cluster than RGB, so thresholding for face and gesture detection is more reliable. Skin-segmentation work still cites it alongside YCbCr and HSV.

space.tsl.use.t: Face and gesture detection in computer vision; niche, still referenced.

space.ucs.desc.t: CIE 1960 UCS is MacAdam's uniform chromaticity space, an early attempt to make equal distances on a chromaticity diagram match equal perceived color differences. Adding a lightness dimension extended it into CIE 1964 U*V*W*; CIELUV superseded it in 1976.

space.ucs.successor-note.t: The CIE stretched its v axis by 1.5 for better uniformity: u′v′

space.uv.desc.t: CIE 1976 UCS (u′, v′) — the more perceptually uniform successor to the 1960 chromaticity diagram, standardized in CIE 15:2004. Equal distances on the u′v′ plane match equal perceived color differences more closely than on CIE xy, which is why white-point tolerances (Δu′v′) and colorimeter reports use it.

space.uv.use.t: LED binning and white-point tolerancing; the standard uniform chromaticity diagram.

space.uvw.desc.t: CIE 1964 U*V*W* is Wyszecki's extension of the CIE 1960 UCS diagram into three dimensions, adding a cube-root lightness axis over the earlier uniform chromaticity coordinates. It was one of several 1960s spaces trying to make Euclidean distance track perceived color difference better than raw XYZ did.

space.uvw.successor-note.t: The CIE adopted CIELUV, built on the improved u′v′ diagram

space.vgamut.desc.t: V-Gamut – Panasonic's camera RGB primaries, introduced in 2014 with the VARICAM 35 and paired with the V-Log curve. Panasonic reached it by tuning the on-chip color filters of the camera's Super 35 sensor and positioned it as a master-archive space, converted to DCI-P3 or BT.709 in post. This is the scene-linear form, before V-Log, with highlights above 1.0.

space.vgamut.use.t: Scene-linear gamut under V-Log for VFX and grading of Panasonic VARICAM and cinema footage.

space.viperlog.desc.t: ViperLog — the log curve of the Thomson Viper FilmStream, one of the earliest digital cinema cameras, announced in 2002. It is a pure log10 with no black offset, a simplicity later curves from other makers corrected to avoid crushing near-black detail. With no published gamut of its own, it is applied over linear-light RGB.

space.viperlog.retired.t: The tapeless RED and ARRI ALEXA workflows came to dominate digital cinema

space.vlog.desc.t: V-Log — Panasonic's log curve, introduced in 2014 with the VARICAM 35 cinema camera to hold the sensor's full dynamic range for grading. It pairs with the wide V-Gamut primaries, built to enclose spaces like Rec. 2020 with room to spare. Panasonic's mirrorless GH bodies use a lighter variant, V-Log L, matched to a narrower 12-stop range.

space.vlog.use.t: Panasonic VARICAM and cinema cameras, with V-Gamut.

space.wavelength.desc.t: Wavelength — the color of monochromatic light, one point on the spectrum of pure hues from deep violet near 380 nm to deep red near 700 nm. The CIE 1931 standard observer's color-matching functions, the measured functions behind all of modern colorimetry, map it to XYZ. The inverse finds the nearest spectral wavelength of any color: the dominant wavelength that gives CIE DSH its hue, projected into 380–700 nm.

space.wavelength.loss-note.t: Any color projects to its nearest spectral-locus hue; purples have no wavelength.

space.wavelength.use.t: Mapping monochromatic light to XYZ through the CIE 1931 standard observer.

space.widegamut.desc.t: Adobe Wide Gamut RGB – a Photoshop working space from Adobe Systems whose primaries sit on or near the spectral locus at 700, 525 and 450 nm, referenced to D50. It encloses 77.6% of the CIELAB gamut in Lindbloom's comparison, against 50.6% for Adobe RGB (1998), so it keeps saturated film and print colors that smaller spaces clip. It shares Adobe RGB (1998)'s 563/256 power-law encoding.

space.xvycc.desc.t: xvYCC (extended-gamut YCC) is Sony's extension of YCbCr to colors outside the BT.601/BT.709 gamut triangle, standardized as IEC 61966-2-4 and marketed as x.v.Color. Legal-range YCbCr clips any signal beyond the primaries it was built around; xvYCC keeps the same luma/chroma structure but allows values past that range, so cameras and displays can carry more saturated colors than SD or HD video normally allows.

space.xvycc.use.t: Consumer camcorders, TVs and Blu-ray recorders (x.v.Color); niche, mostly superseded by HDR formats.

space.xyb.desc.t: XYB is the internal color space of JPEG XL, the royalty-free successor to JPEG for lossy and lossless compression. Where JPEG builds on broadcast-derived YCbCr, XYB models the eye's LMS cone responses as a red-green channel (X), a luminance channel (Y) and a blue-yellow channel (B), compressed with a perceptual power law so coding error lands where vision is least sensitive.

space.xyb.use.t: Compression inside the JPEG XL codec.

space.xyy.desc.t: xyY — CIE XYZ rewritten as chromaticity (x, y) plus luminance (Y), so hue and saturation can be studied apart from brightness. Plotting x against y gives the familiar horseshoe-shaped chromaticity diagram.

space.xyz-abs-d65.desc.t: Absolute XYZ (D65) — CIE XYZ in candela per square meter instead of the usual relative 0–100 scale. Relative XYZ only compares a color to a normalized white; absolute XYZ ties each value to measurable luminance, which HDR needs, since one relative color can sit at very different real luminances. The two scales meet at ITU-R BT.2100's HDR reference white.

space.xyz-abs-d65.use.t: HDR analysis tools; anchored to BT.2100's 203 cd/m² reference white.

space.xyz-d50.desc.t: CIE XYZ referred to the D50 illuminant instead of D65. It is the profile connection space ICC profiles convert through, a convention from graphic-arts and print viewing standards, and Bradford chromatic adaptation relates it to D65 XYZ.

space.xyz.desc.t: CIE XYZ — the foundation of modern colorimetry, defined by the CIE in 1931 from the standard observer's color-matching functions. X, Y and Z are not perceptual attributes; they are engineered so that Y alone carries luminance, X and Z carry chromaticity, and any visible color is a weighted sum of three fixed imaginary primaries. RGB, Lab and other working spaces are defined against it.

space.xyz.use.t: The device-independent reference underlying all colorimetry.

space.ycbcr-bt2020.desc.t: ITU-R BT.2020 non-constant-luminance Y′CbCr — the explicit studio-range digital component encoding for UHDTV. It uses Rec.2020 primaries/OETF, Kr=0.2627, Kb=0.0593, and 8-bit legal ranges Y′ 16–235, Cb/Cr 16–240. This is the common non-constant-luminance form, distinct from the library's `yccbccrc` constant-luminance representation.

space.ycbcr-bt2020.use.t: UHDTV and wide-gamut codecs, as unambiguous limited-range Y′CbCr.

space.ycbcr-bt601-525.desc.t: ITU-R BT.601 Y′CbCr for 525-line systems — the studio-range digital component encoding used by NTSC-derived standard-definition video. It combines the BT.601 luma coefficients Kr=0.299 and Kb=0.114 with SMPTE-C primaries and 8-bit legal code ranges (Y′ 16–235, Cb/Cr 16–240).

space.ycbcr-bt601-525.use.t: NTSC-family SD video, as unambiguous BT.601 Y′CbCr.

space.ycbcr-bt601-625.desc.t: ITU-R BT.601 Y′CbCr for 625-line systems — the studio-range digital component encoding used by PAL/SECAM-derived standard-definition video. It combines the BT.601 luma coefficients Kr=0.299 and Kb=0.114 with EBU/PAL primaries and 8-bit legal code ranges (Y′ 16–235, Cb/Cr 16–240).

space.ycbcr-bt601-625.use.t: PAL-family SD video, as unambiguous BT.601 Y′CbCr.

space.ycbcr-bt709.desc.t: ITU-R BT.709 Y′CbCr is a digital video encoding for HDTV. It uses BT.709 primaries and OETF, with fixed coefficients Kr=0.2126 and Kb=0.0722. The 8-bit code ranges are Y′ 16–235 and Cb/Cr 16–240.

space.ycbcr-bt709.use.t: HDTV production, broadcast and codecs, as unambiguous BT.709 Y′CbCr.

space.ycbcr.desc.t: YCbCr is the digital luma/chroma format behind almost all broadcast and compressed video, standardized by the ITU-R as BT.601 for standard definition and BT.709 for high definition. Like analog YUV before it and YPbPr, its analog counterpart, it pairs a luma channel Y that alone gives a usable grayscale image with blue- and red-difference chroma Cb and Cr, but in a digital studio (“limited”) range that reserves headroom and footroom for processing overshoot.

space.ycbcr.use.t: Broadcast and compressed video (BT.601/709): DVD, H.264, HEVC.

space.yccbccrc.desc.t: YcCbcCrc is the constant-luminance encoding defined in ITU-R BT.2020 for UHD wide-gamut video; for HDR, BT.2100 offers ICtCp instead. Ordinary Y′CbCr takes luma from gamma-encoded RGB, so saturated colors leak into luma and distort perceived brightness, more visibly at the wider gamuts and higher dynamic range BT.2020 and BT.2100 target. YcCbcCrc takes luma from linear light before the transfer curve, keeping brightness and chroma separate even for the most saturated colors.

space.yccbccrc.use.t: UHDTV wide-gamut video (BT.2020); less common than non-constant-luminance Y′CbCr.

space.ycgco.desc.t: YCgCo is a luma/chroma transform Malvar and Sullivan introduced in 2003, cheap to compute and exact to invert. Cg and Co are green- and orange-difference chroma, built from RGB with lighter arithmetic than YCbCr's coefficients.

space.ycgco.use.t: Specific coding modes of H.264/AVC and HEVC.

space.ycxcz.desc.t: YyCxCz is a linearized CIELAB from model-based halftoning, by Flohr, Kolpatzik, Balasubramanian, Carrara, Bouman and Allebach (1993). It keeps CIELAB's white normalization and scale factors and drops the cube root: Yy = 116·Y/Yn − 16, Cx = 500·(X/Xn − Y/Yn), Cz = 200·(Y/Yn − Z/Zn). Being linear in XYZ, its channels can be low-pass filtered like light, so halftone error models and image-difference metrics such as NVIDIA's FLIP filter here before converting to CIELAB.

space.ycxcz.use.t: Halftone design and spatial image-difference metrics (FLIP): filter here, then go to CIELAB.

space.ydbdr.desc.t: YDbDr is the luma/chroma encoding of SECAM (“Séquentiel Couleur à Mémoire”), the analog color TV standard developed in France and adopted in parts of Eastern Europe, the former Soviet Union and Africa. Like YUV for PAL and YIQ for NTSC, it keeps a luma channel Y for monochrome sets and adds two scaled color differences, Db from blue minus luma and Dr from red minus luma.

space.ydbdr.use.t: Analog SECAM television in France, Eastern Europe and the former USSR; historical.

space.ydzdx.desc.t: Y′D′zD′x is the luma and color-difference form of PQ-encoded CIE XYZ, standardized by SMPTE as ST 2085 in 2015 and listed in ITU-T H.273 as matrix coefficients 11. Absolute X, Y, Z are each encoded with the SMPTE ST 2084 (PQ) inverse EOTF; Y′ passes through and D′z, D′x are weighted differences of Z′ and X′ against Y′, tuned so D65 at 500 cd/m² has zero color difference.

space.yes.desc.t: YES is a luminance/chrominance encoding in the same family as YIQ and YUV, defined in Xerox's Color Encoding Standard (XNSS 289005, 1989). Y, E (green-red) and S (blue-yellow) are simple linear combinations of R, G and B; their appeal is that they are cheap to compute, but unlike CIELAB or CIELUV they are not perceptually uniform, so equal steps in E or S do not look equal. The imaging literature lists it among encodings for image analysis and compression.

space.yes.use.t: The Xerox Color Encoding Standard; historical, niche in imaging literature.

space.yiq.desc.t: YIQ is the luma/chroma encoding adopted for NTSC color television in the United States in 1953, to add color without breaking the millions of black-and-white sets already in homes. Y alone gives the black-and-white picture; I and Q carry chroma on axes rotated from YUV's blue- and red-difference ones, because the eye is more sensitive along orange-cyan than green-purple, which lets Q take less bandwidth.

space.yiq.successor-note.t: Digital video carries color as YCbCr, with no analog subcarrier to modulate

space.yiq.use.t: The original US NTSC analog color TV.

space.ypbpr.desc.t: YPbPr is the analog component-video counterpart to digital YCbCr: the same luma plus color-difference structure, carried over three separate analog cables. Y alone gives a grayscale picture; Pb and Pr are blue- and red-difference chroma scaled to a standard analog range. It is defined alongside ITU-R BT.709 for HD and BT.601 for SD, and was the higher-quality analog connection before HDMI.

space.ypbpr.use.t: DVD players, consoles and HDTVs before HDMI; displaced by digital.

space.yrg.desc.t: Yrg — Richard Kirk's 2019 luminance/chromaticity space, built at FilmLight on CIE 2006 cone fundamentals and tuned so hues sit evenly around the wheel, matching the classical Munsell order. Y is cone-weighted luminance; r and g are chromaticity coordinates derived affinely from the cone responses, which keeps brightness apart from hue and saturation.

space.yrg.use.t: Color grading, as the basis of darktable's color-balance module; niche.

space.yuv.desc.t: YUV is the analog color encoding developed for PAL television. Color rides alongside the black-and-white signal without breaking monochrome receivers: Y alone carries brightness, and U and V add scaled blue- and red-difference chroma. Splitting luma from chroma let broadcasters spend less bandwidth on color than on brightness, since the eye sees less chroma detail.

space.yuv.use.t: Analog PAL television; historical, though “YUV” is now used loosely for digital video too.

space.zcam.desc.t: ZCAM is the color appearance model Safdar, Hardeberg and Luo introduced in 2021, designed for high dynamic range and wide gamut from the start. Like CAM16 it predicts lightness, colorfulness and hue under given viewing conditions, but it builds on the absolute Izazbz space, not CIE XYZ, so it works in the absolute luminance HDR needs, where older models assume a relative 0–100 scale. It also reports brightness, vividness, blackness and whiteness.

space.zcam.use.t: HDR display calibration and gamut mapping; active in research and tools.

term.adaptation.tip.t: the re-balancing of colors when the light source changes, so white stays white

term.chromaticity.tip.t: color with luminance factored out – the (x, y) spot on the CIE horseshoe

term.difference.tip.t: how far apart two colors look – ΔE metrics score it; the smallest visible step is about 1–2 in ΔE2000, 2.3 in ΔE76, 0.02 in Oklab

term.dynamic-range.tip.t: the luminance span between the darkest and brightest values a signal can carry

term.eotf.tip.t: electro-optical transfer function – code value in, display light out (the display curve)

term.gamut-mapping.tip.t: squeezing colors a display cannot show into its reachable set without breaking the image

term.illuminant.tip.t: the standardized light source a space assumes – D65 daylight, D50 print viewing, E equal energy

term.observer.tip.t: the CIE-averaged human eye – the color-matching functions colorimetry is built on

term.oetf.tip.t: opto-electronic transfer function – scene light in, code value out (the camera curve)

term.pq.tip.t: perceptual quantizer (SMPTE ST 2084) – the absolute-luminance HDR curve, up to 10,000 nits

term.scene-linear.tip.t: values proportional to physical light in the scene, before any display encoding

term.uniform.tip.t: equal numeric steps look like equal color steps – distance in the space matches what eyes report

term.untagged.tip.t: images with no embedded color profile – browsers assume they are sRGB

term.white-point.tip.t: the reference white a space adapts to – D65 ≈ daylight, D50 ≈ print viewing, E = equal energy

tip.historical.t: superseded in practice, kept faithful to the original
